Freelance Bookkeeping

Bookkeeping is one of the lowest-friction service businesses you can start: no inventory, no storefront, free core tooling, and clients who pay you every single month to keep their books clean. It is unglamorous on purpose. The boredom is the moat.

Why this niche works

Every business that takes money has to track that money. The US payroll & bookkeeping services market was about 76500000000 in 2025, and roughly 1600000 people already do this work as employees. The interesting part: BLS projects employee clerk roles to decline about 6 percent from 2024 to 2034 as software automates data entry — yet about 170000 openings appear each year, and a growing share of the actual work shifts to outsourced freelancers and fractional firms.

That is the wedge. Small businesses do not want a full-time hire; they want someone reliable to own the books for a flat monthly fee.

The economics

  • Median for employed clerks: about 49210 USD/year (May 2024). That is your floor, not your ceiling — it is the salary you are competing against, and freelancing lets you stack clients past it.
  • Average freelance rate: around 22.75 USD/hour as a blended national average, but experienced operators in high-cost metros routinely charge $40-65/hour, and most successful solo bookkeepers move off hourly to flat monthly retainers ($300-$1,000+/client) precisely because hourly punishes you for getting faster.
  • The retainer math: 15 clients at a mid-range ~$500/month is roughly $90,000/year gross from a laptop. That is the SOM figure above, and it is conservative — many solos cap higher per client or add advisory/payroll/cleanup work.

Saturation reality check

This niche scores ~62/100 on saturation: easy to enter, so there is real competition, but demand is structural and the move to outsourced books is a tailwind. The losers compete on being "cheaper QuickBooks data entry." The winners pick a vertical (e-commerce, trades, restaurants, agencies, real estate investors), learn that industry's chart of accounts and tax quirks cold, and become the obvious choice for that one type of business. Niche beats generalist here every time.

How to start (step by step)

  • Get the free credential first. Open a free QuickBooks Online Accountant account and complete the QuickBooks ProAdvisor certification — it costs $0 and takes roughly 8 hours plus testing. This is the single highest-ROI move because it gets you free software access and a directory listing where clients search for bookkeepers.
  • Decide on a vertical. Do not say "I do bookkeeping for everyone." Pick one industry you understand or can study (e.g., Shopify sellers, plumbers/HVAC, dental offices). Specialization lets you charge more and market faster.
  • Stand up the legal/operational basics. Register your business (sole prop or LLC depending on your situation and state), open a separate business bank account, and get a simple engagement-letter template and proposal tool. Budget roughly $500 all-in for setup.
  • Build a one-page offer, not a pricing menu. Define a flat monthly package: "I categorize your transactions, reconcile your accounts, and send you a clean P&L and balance sheet every month for $X." Flat pricing wins SMB clients who fear hourly surprises.
  • Land your first 1-3 clients through warm + niche channels. Tell every business owner you already know. Then post in the vertical's communities (industry Facebook groups, subreddits, local BNI/chamber). Offer a paid "catch-up / cleanup" project as a low-risk entry that converts to a monthly retainer.
  • Deliver a flawless first close, then ask for the referral. Your first month is your marketing. Reconcile to the penny, deliver on time, and explain the numbers in plain English. Bookkeeping referrals compound because trust with someone's money is hard-won and freely passed along.
  • Systematize and raise prices. Once you have repeatable processes (standard onboarding checklist, monthly close checklist, client portal), each new client costs you less time. Raise rates on new clients first, then grandfather increases for existing ones. Consider the AIPB Certified Bookkeeper (CB) credential (about $100 per part, four parts) once you want a recognized professional designation beyond software certs.

Where it goes from here

Solo bookkeeping is the on-ramp. The same client relationship lets you layer in payroll, accounts-payable management, monthly advisory calls, and eventually a small team or fractional-CFO services — each step raising your revenue per client without needing more clients. Start boring, stay reliable, and let the monthly checks compound.

Freelance Copywriting

Copywriting is writing words that get someone to act: buy, sign up, click, book a call. It is one of the cleanest service businesses you can start because the only required input is skill, the output is digital, and almost every business with something to sell needs it. The global copywriting services market was about 25290000000 in 2023 and is projected to reach 42220000000 by 2030, a 7.6% CAGR. That growth is being pulled by the same force everywhere: more businesses, more channels, more content to fill.

Why this niche

  • Near-zero startup cost. You can launch for roughly 200. No inventory, no license, no premises.
  • Fast first dollar. A first paid gig is realistically 14 days out if you already write competently.
  • Real income ceiling. US freelance copywriters average around 65000 per year, but that average hides the spread: rate data shows novices around $26-29/hr and experienced writers commanding $75-125/hr. The money is in conversion-focused work (sales pages, email sequences, ads), not blog filler.
  • AI-resistant at the top. Generic prose is now a commodity that AI tools produce cheaply, which is exactly why the floor is crowded. Copy that is tied to a measurable business result (a sales page that lifts conversion, an email sequence that recovers carts) still pays, because the client is buying outcomes, not word count. Upwork's 2024 demand notes flag persuasive, conversion-oriented writing as the durable corner of the field.

The honest downside

Saturation is high (scored ~72/100). The barrier to entry that makes it easy for you makes it easy for everyone, and the bottom of the market is being eaten by AI. The realistic single-operator capture (SOM) is roughly 80000 in revenue within the first year or two, and reaching that requires niching down and selling results, not "I write good." Generalist, by-the-word copywriting is a race to the bottom. Specialists win.

How to start: step-by-step

  • Pick one niche and one format. Not "copywriter." Instead: "email sequences for e-commerce skincare brands" or "sales pages for B2B SaaS." A specific buyer with budget and a recurring need is the whole game. Niching down is the single biggest lever on your rate.
  • Build 2-3 spec samples. You do not need paying clients to have a portfolio. Rewrite a real company's weak sales page or write a sample email sequence for a brand you admire. Make them excellent and put them on a one-page site.
  • Set up the minimum business stack. A domain, a professional email, a simple portfolio site (Carrd, a Notion page, or a one-pager), and an invoicing tool. Keep it under your startup budget; do not over-build before you have a client.
  • Learn the persuasion fundamentals. Read and dissect proven sales copy. Study frameworks (AIDA, PAS, the 4 Ps). Understand that good copy starts with research into the customer's pain, not with clever wording.
  • Land the first three clients through warm channels. Tell your existing network exactly what you do and for whom. Post your spec work publicly. Use marketplaces (Upwork, Contra) only to get reps and a review, not as your long-term home; the rates there are suppressed by competition.
  • Price by value or retainer, never by the word. Word-rate pricing caps your income and signals commodity. Quote a project fee tied to the deliverable's importance, or move clients onto a monthly retainer for ongoing email/content work. Retainers are how you get predictable revenue.
  • Get a result, then get a testimonial with a number. "Increased their email open rate from 18% to 31%" is worth ten generic five-star reviews. One measurable win lets you raise rates and attract better clients.
  • Raise rates and specialize harder. Once you are booked, increase prices on new clients, drop the lowest-paying work, and deepen into the highest-value format in your niche. This is how you move from the $30/hr average toward the $75-125/hr experienced tier.

Bottom line

Freelance copywriting is a low-cost, fast-to-launch service business in a growing market, but it is crowded and AI is compressing the generic end. The winners are not "writers for hire." They are specialists who sell measurable business outcomes to a specific, paying buyer. Pick a niche, prove a result, price on value.

Freelance Graphic Design

Graphic design is one of the lowest-friction creative service businesses you can start: a laptop, design software, and a small portfolio are enough to take on paying work. The flip side is that the same low barrier means the generalist end is crowded. The freelancers who win in 2026 are the ones who pick a sharp niche and sell outcomes (more conversions, a stronger brand) rather than "I make logos."

Is the market big enough?

Yes, and it is still growing. The global graphic design market was valued at roughly 65.62 billion USD in 2025 and is forecast to keep expanding at a mid-single-digit CAGR through the early 2030s. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 265,900 graphic designers in 2024, with a median annual wage of 61,300 USD. Around 18 percent of them are self-employed, which tells you freelancing is a normal, proven path in this field.

Demand outlook is mixed and worth being honest about: BLS projects only about 2 percent employment growth for graphic designers from 2024 to 2034 (slower than average), yet roughly 20,000 openings appear each year from churn. AI design tools are simultaneously expanding the pie (more businesses producing more content) and compressing the floor for commodity work. The takeaway: the money is moving toward designers with taste, strategy, and a niche.

What you can actually earn

Average freelance graphic designer rates sit near 49.65 USD per hour in 2025. That is an average, not a ceiling. Beginners on open marketplaces often start at $15-$35/hr, while specialists working directly with clients routinely command $65-$150+/hr. Your rate is mostly a function of niche clarity and proof, not years served.

Saturation reality check

Saturation score: 72 / 100 (high). The generalist "logos and flyers" tier is brutally competitive thanks to global marketplace supply and AI tools. But saturation is uneven: brand identity for funded startups, packaging design, pitch-deck and investor-document design, motion/social-video graphics, and design for regulated industries (healthcare, finance) all have far thinner competition and higher willingness to pay. Pick a lane.

Costs to start

You can start lean. A home-based setup typically runs about 3,000 USD (capable computer, software, basic marketing), and the full range across business plans is roughly $2,000-$10,000 depending on hardware. The recurring cost that matters most is software:

  • Adobe Creative Cloud Pro (All Apps): about 69.99 USD per month.
  • Adobe Photography plan (Photoshop + Lightroom): about 19.99 USD per month.
  • Free / low-cost alternatives: Figma, Canva, Inkscape, GIMP, and one-time-purchase tools like Affinity let you start at near-zero software cost.

If you take marketplace work, budget for platform fees too: Upwork moved from a flat 10% to a 0 to 15 percent variable freelancer service fee in May 2025, with most freelancers effectively paying around 10%.

Time to first dollar

Realistically 1-3 weeks if you already have basic skills. The bottleneck is not skill, it is proof and reach: you need a few portfolio pieces and you need people to know you exist. Marketplaces shorten this (you can win a gig in days); direct clients pay more but take longer to land.

Step-by-step: how to start

  • Pick ONE niche before anything else. Not "graphic design" - pick "Shopify product-page graphics for skincare brands" or "pitch decks for pre-seed SaaS." A niche makes your marketing, portfolio, and pricing 10x easier and pulls you out of the saturated generalist pool.
  • Set up your tools. Start with what is free or cheap (Figma + Canva + Affinity, or the Adobe Photography plan) and only upgrade to full Creative Cloud Pro once paid work justifies the ~$70/month.
  • Build a 3-5 piece portfolio in your niche. Real or self-initiated "spec" projects both work. Quality and relevance beat quantity. Show before/after and the business outcome, not just pretty pixels.
  • Define your offer and price. Productize: name 2-3 concrete packages with fixed scope and price (e.g., "Brand Starter Kit," "Pitch Deck Redesign"). Fixed-scope packages convert better and protect your hourly economics versus open-ended hourly work.
  • Set up the business basics. A simple portfolio site or Behance/Dribbble profile, an invoicing tool, a contract template, and a way to take payment. Register as a sole proprietor or LLC per your state's rules (see the operations pillar).
  • Get your first clients through your warm network first. Tell everyone you know exactly what you do and for whom. Referrals and warm intros close faster and at higher rates than cold marketplace bids.
  • Add ONE outbound channel. Either a marketplace (Upwork/Contra/Fiverr) for speed, or targeted cold outreach/DMs to businesses in your niche for margin. Do one well before adding a second.
  • Deliver, then ask for a testimonial and a referral every single time. Social proof compounds. Three strong testimonials in a niche will out-sell a giant generic portfolio.
  • Raise rates as your queue fills. When you are booked out 2+ weeks, raise prices on new clients by 15-25%. Repeat. Use AI tools to speed production so your effective hourly rate climbs while your price stays competitive.

Common failure modes to avoid

  • Staying a generalist to "keep options open" - this keeps you in the saturated, low-paid tier forever.
  • Charging hourly for everything - you get punished for being fast. Productize and price on value.
  • Skipping contracts and deposits - scope creep and non-payment are the two biggest cash killers for new freelancers.
  • Competing with AI on speed instead of using it - AI is a force multiplier for the designer who brings taste and strategy.

Bottom line

Freelance graphic design is a real, proven business with a large and growing global market, but the generalist entry tier is saturated. Win by niching hard, productizing your offer, charging on outcomes, and using AI to widen your margins. Low startup cost (~$3,000) and fast time-to-first-dollar (1-3 weeks) make it one of the most accessible service businesses to test quickly.

Furniture Assembly Service

Flat-pack furniture is everywhere, and a growing share of buyers do not want to spend their Saturday wrestling with an Allen wrench and a 40-page diagram. That gap is a business. Furniture assembly is one of the lowest-barrier service niches you can start this week: the only hard requirements are a drill, reliability, and the willingness to read instructions carefully.

Why this niche works

Online furniture sales in the US neared 125000000000 in 2024, and roughly 31 percent of shoppers buy household furniture online monthly. Almost all of it ships flat-packed. Every one of those boxes is a potential job.

The dedicated assembly-and-disassembly services market was valued at 1974700000 globally in 2025 and is forecast to grow at 5.9 percent annually through 2035. North America leads, worth about 600000000 in 2024. Big retail is leaning in too: in May 2025 The Home Depot signed Handy to provide in-home assembly across the US, signaling the demand is durable, not a fad.

The money

Pricing is per-item or hourly, and it is better than most people assume.

  • National average is about 150 per piece, with a common range of $50-$150.
  • Handyperson hourly rates average around 90 per hour (range $40-$140).
  • By item: end tables $40-$100, chairs $40-$160, beds $70-$160, dressers $100-$350, entertainment centers $100-$350.
  • Platform floors: TaskRabbit assembly often starts at a 52 minimum, with large/complex items starting near $150.

A confident assembler can finish 3-5 small-to-medium pieces in a day. At even $80-$120 per piece, that is real daily revenue against near-zero material cost.

Saturation reality check

This niche scores moderate-to-high on saturation: platforms and general handymen already compete for the work. But two things keep it open. First, demand consistently outpaces reliable supply in most local markets, especially for evenings and weekends. Second, the business is won on reviews, speed, and showing up on time, which a focused solo operator can do better than a stretched-thin handyman who treats assembly as filler work. Specialize, be the person who answers the phone, and you win.

Startup cost and time-to-first-dollar

  • Startup cost: roughly $200 on the low end (drill, hand tools, free platform signup) to $1,500 with a pro kit, hand truck, an LLC, and liability insurance.
  • Time to first dollar: as little as a few days. Sign up on a platform, set availability, and accept the first job. Off-platform, your first dollar comes as soon as a neighbor or local-group post converts.

How to start: step by step

  • Buy the core kit. A good cordless drill/driver, a bit set, an Allen-key set (metric and SAE), a rubber mallet, a level, and a utility knife. Add an impact driver and a hand truck as you scale. Budget $150-$400 for a solid starter set.
  • Practice on real flat-packs. Assemble two or three IKEA-style pieces (a desk, a dresser, a bookshelf) for friends or yourself. Time yourself. This builds speed and surfaces the gotchas (cam locks, dowel orientation, hidden hardware) before a paying customer is watching.
  • List on a platform first. Create a TaskRabbit and/or Handy profile to get instant lead flow and your first reviews. Accept the platform's per-item or hourly pricing initially to win bookings and ratings fast.
  • Set your own pricing. Anchor to local benchmarks: roughly $40-$60 for small items, $80-$120 for medium, $120-$200+ for large/complex. Charge a minimum trip fee (e.g., $50-$75) so small jobs are still worth the drive.
  • Go off-platform to keep the full cut. Platforms take a fee. Post in local Facebook groups, Nextdoor, and to apartment-complex managers and movers. A simple "same-week furniture assembly, fully insured, 5-star rated" pitch with photos converts.
  • Build the review flywheel. Ask every happy customer for a review and a referral the moment the job is done. Reviews are the entire moat in this niche; treat each one as inventory.
  • Formalize and protect yourself. Once you have steady work, register an LLC and carry general liability insurance. Customers paying $150+ to enter their home expect a real business, and insurance both protects you and closes more jobs.
  • Productize and add-on. Offer disassembly for movers, wall-mounting (TVs, shelves, mirrors), and "white-glove" packages (assemble + haul away the boxes). These raise your average ticket without adding marketing cost.
  • Schedule for the demand. Evenings and weekends are when people are home and boxes are waiting. Make those your prime hours and charge accordingly.

Where it can go

Solo, this is a reliable five-figure side income. Hire and train one or two assemblers, add commercial accounts (offices, staging companies, property managers, movers), and it becomes a small local services brand. The same tools and trust extend naturally into general handyman work, mounting, and small installs, so furniture assembly is also a low-risk on-ramp to a broader home-services business.

Game Streaming and Content

Game streaming is broadcasting yourself playing — or talking, building, or creating — live to an audience on Twitch, YouTube, Kick, or all three at once, and turning watch time into income through subscriptions, ads, donations, and sponsorships. The appeal is real: the gear can be cheap, the platform is free, and a genuinely entertaining person with a consistent schedule can build a small business out of a spare bedroom. The hard part is not technical. It is the discovery math, which is brutal.

The opportunity at a glance

The global game streaming market was expected to reach USD 12.00 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 12.9% through 2033 — that is your TAM, but most of it flows to platforms, advertisers, and esports orgs, not to individual broadcasters.

The slice a solo creator actually competes for is the creator-payout economy on the dominant platform. Twitch alone generated roughly USD 1.8 billion in revenue in 2025, against a base of about 240 million monthly active users. A large share of that revenue is shared back to creators through subscriptions and ads — that shared pool, plus off-platform sponsorships and YouTube ad revenue, is the realistic SAM you can earn a living from.

Saturation: 88/100

Be honest with yourself about this number. Streaming is one of the most saturated niches in this entire catalog. The barrier to entry is near zero, so everyone is in, and the audience's attention is distributed in an extreme winner-take-most curve: a thin top layer of channels captures the overwhelming majority of watch hours, while the long tail averages a handful of viewers or fewer. You are not competing for a fair share of 240 million people — you are competing for the few who happen to find you before the algorithm buries you under thousands of channels playing the same game.

That does not make it hopeless. It makes differentiation non-optional. The creators who break out almost never win by streaming a popular game competently; they win on personality, a niche game or format nobody else owns, a clippable hook, off-platform funnels (TikTok/Shorts clips that drive to the live channel), or a community they cultivate by name. Treat the live stream as the campfire and short-form clips as the road signs that lead people to it.

Economics that make it work

  • Startup cost: ~$350. Assuming you already own a capable gaming PC or console, the streaming kit is cheap. A budget USB microphone runs roughly $60 to $100, a 1080p webcam $50-70, a light $30-50, decent headphones $40-60, and a controller/stream deck plus cables rounds it out. You can genuinely start under $300 with budget kits and add gear as revenue arrives. The software (OBS Studio) is free.
  • Two monetization gates. Twitch's Affiliate tier is the first money: hit 50 followers, 500 broadcast minutes, 7 unique stream days, and 3 average concurrent viewers in a rolling 30-day window and the invite is automatic. The default subscription split is 50/50 — Twitch keeps half of each ~$4.99 sub. The improved 70/30 split only unlocks through the Partner Plus program after sustaining hundreds of paid subs for three consecutive months, so plan your early math around 50/50.
  • Time to first dollar: ~60 days. All four Affiliate requirements are measured against the same rolling 30-day window, so the clock genuinely resets if you hit them at different times. A focused beginner who streams a fixed schedule and drives traffic with clips typically clears the bar and earns a first payout (NET 15, $50 minimum) inside one to two months.
  • Income is a portfolio, not a salary. No serious streamer lives on subs alone. The durable channels stack subscriptions, bits/donations, mid-roll ads, channel memberships, sponsorships, affiliate links, and a YouTube VOD/clips channel that earns its own ad revenue and recruits new live viewers.

How to start: step by step

  • Pick a defensible angle before you buy anything. Choose a game or format where you can be a top-100 channel, not a bottom-10,000 one in a flooded category. A mid-popularity game, a unique format (speedruns, challenge runs, co-streaming with a bit), or a strong on-camera persona beats "good at a popular game" every time. Write down in one sentence why a stranger would stay.
  • Assemble the minimum kit. Download OBS Studio (free). Add a USB mic, a webcam, a light, and headphones — roughly $350 total per the gear breakdown above. Do not buy a second monitor, a green screen, or a $300 mic on day one; upgrade after the channel earns.
  • Build your scenes and overlays. In OBS, set up at least a "Starting Soon," "Live," and "Be Right Back" scene. Use a free or cheap overlay pack. Set your bitrate and resolution to what your upload speed can sustain reliably — a stable 720p60 beats a stuttering 1080p every time.
  • Set a fixed schedule and publish it. Consistency is the single biggest lever for a new channel. Pick specific days and times (e.g., Tue/Thu/Sat 7-10pm) and put them on your channel panels. Viewers and the algorithm both reward predictability.
  • Stream to grow the four Affiliate metrics deliberately. You need 50 followers, 500 minutes, 7 unique days, and 3 avg concurrent viewers in one 30-day window. Talk constantly even to zero viewers (the VOD is your audition), engage every single chatter by name, and never sit silent.
  • Run a short-form clip funnel from day one. Pull your best 20-60 second moments into TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Reels with a "live now" call to action. For a tiny channel, clips are usually a bigger growth source than the live discovery feed itself.
  • Hit Affiliate, then turn on monetization. Once invited, enable subs, bits, and ads, and connect your payout method. Expect 50/50 on subs at this stage; treat the 70/30 Partner Plus tier as a later milestone, not a starting assumption.
  • Diversify and reinvest. Add a YouTube channel for VODs and clips (its own ad revenue plus a discovery engine), pursue your first small sponsorships once you have a stable concurrent viewership, and reinvest early earnings into the upgrades — better mic, capture card, second PC — that visibly raise production quality.

The honest bottom line

The market is large and growing, the tools are cheap, and the path to your first dollar is clearly defined. But the 88/100 saturation is the number that decides whether this becomes income or a hobby. Win on a defensible angle, a relentless schedule, and a clip funnel that brings strangers to your campfire — or accept that "stream a popular game and hope" is, mathematically, a lottery ticket.

Garage Epoxy Flooring

Garage epoxy flooring is one of the cleanest entry points into the home-services trades: low capital, high ticket, repeatable scope, and a customer who has already decided they want it before they call you. A homeowner pays for a bare concrete slab to become a glossy, flaked, easy-to-clean surface that makes the most-used room in the house feel finished. The work is teachable in weeks, the materials are commodity, and the margin lives almost entirely in two things you control: surface prep and finish quality.

Why this niche

The global garage flooring market was valued at roughly USD 17.56B in 2026, growing at about 5.5% per year, with North America holding the largest regional slice at 38.3%. Epoxy is the workhorse chemistry of that market — about 32.8% of global garage-flooring revenue and the leading floor-coating chemistry in the US at over 42% of the domestic floor-coatings market.

Translation for an operator: this is a real, growing, multi-billion-dollar category, but it is delivered one driveway at a time by local crews. National statistics do not protect an incumbent. A sharp solo operator who shows up on time, preps the slab correctly, and posts before/after photos can take share in any metro.

The money math

Homeowners typically pay $4-$12 per square foot for a professional epoxy/flake/polyaspartic system, and the national average for a coated garage floor lands around $2,227, with most jobs between $1,447 and $3,006. A standard two-car garage (400-500 sq ft) is a one-day job for a competent two-person crew. Your direct material cost on a flake system is commonly a few hundred dollars per garage, so the gross margin is high once your prep is dialed in. The constraint is not demand — it is how many slabs you can prep and coat per week without callbacks.

What you actually sell

You are not selling "paint." You are selling a system and a guarantee:

  • Single-day full-flake systems (epoxy basecoat + broadcast vinyl flake + polyaspartic/polyurea topcoat) are the premium product most one-day "garage floor" companies push.
  • Metallic epoxy is the upsell finish; flake adds about $1-$3/sq ft and metallic adds about $2-$5/sq ft over a base coat per HomeGuide pricing.
  • Prep and repair (grinding, crack/joint fill, moisture testing) is where amateurs fail. A floor that peels in a year is a refund and a one-star review. Do prep right and you will out-earn cheaper competitors who skip it.

Startup cost and time-to-first-dollar

A lean start runs about $7,000-$25,000 depending on whether you buy or rent the grinder. The big-ticket items are a concrete grinder with a dust shroud, an industrial HEPA vacuum, mixing drills/paddles, broadcast and squeegee tools, PPE, and your first material lots. You can be doing paid work in roughly three weeks: most of that window is registering the business, binding general-liability insurance, and practicing on one slab before you charge for one.

How to start (step by step)

  • Pick your product and master one system. Choose a single full-flake epoxy + polyaspartic system from one reputable manufacturer and learn it cold before you offer three options. One system done perfectly beats five done adequately.
  • Buy the grinder, not the shortcut. The number-one reason coatings fail is bad prep. A diamond grinder (rent first if cash is tight) plus a HEPA vacuum is non-negotiable. Acid etching is not a substitute for grinding on a garage you want to warranty.
  • Register the business and get insured. Form an LLC, get an EIN, and bind general-liability insurance before you touch a customer's property. Check your state and city for any contractor licensing thresholds.
  • Practice on a free or your-own slab. Do your own garage or a friend's at cost. Photograph every stage. This is your first portfolio and your training rep.
  • Build a proof-driven online presence. A simple website, a Google Business Profile, and a feed of real before/after photos. In home services, photos and reviews sell — not adjectives.
  • Price for prep, quote in person, and hold a minimum. Quote per square foot but enforce a job minimum so small garages stay profitable. Inspect for moisture, cracks, and oil staining on the visit and price the repair into the bid.
  • Nail the first ten jobs and farm reviews. Over-communicate, show up on time, leave the garage cleaner than you found it, and ask every happy customer for a Google review and a referral. Your first ten five-star reviews are worth more than your first ad budget.
  • Systematize, then add a crew. Once you are turning away work, document your prep-to-cure checklist and bring on a second person so you can run more slabs per week — that throughput, not price, is your real growth lever.

Risks and how to beat them

  • Callbacks from bad prep. The single biggest profit killer. Grind every floor, fix the cracks, test for moisture. Warranty work eats margin and reputation.
  • Race-to-the-bottom pricing. New operators undercut on price and learn they cannot afford proper materials. Compete on finish quality, durability, and photos instead.
  • Weather and cure windows. Coatings are temperature- and humidity-sensitive. Build cure time into the schedule and do not rush a topcoat.
  • Commodity perception. Customers cannot tell good epoxy from bad until it fails. Your defensible moat is a documented prep process, a real warranty, and a wall of verified reviews.

Bottom line

Saturation is real (competitors and franchises exist in most metros), but the work is delivered locally and quality varies wildly — which is exactly the gap a disciplined operator exploits. Low startup cost, high ticket, one-day jobs, and a buyer who already wants the product. Win on prep and proof, not on price.

Google Ads Management

Google Ads management is the service of running paid-search (and Performance Max, Display, YouTube, Shopping) campaigns for a business owner who does not want to learn the platform themselves. You don't pay for their ads. You charge a fee to plan, build, monitor, and optimize the account so their money converts. It is one of the cleanest service businesses to start because the demand is enormous, the deliverable is measurable in dollars, and you need zero inventory.

Why this niche is real

  • Around 7 million businesses use Google Ads as their primary advertising source 7 million, and roughly 65% of small-to-midsized businesses run PPC 65%. Most of them are bad at it.
  • The platform is credited with a roughly 200% ROI — about $2 back for every $1 spent 200% — which means when you make a client's account work, the fee pays for itself and the relationship sticks.
  • Google's own 2025 ad revenue was about $294.68 billion 294.68 billion, and US digital ad spend sits around $171.33 billion 171.33 billion — the river of money flowing past you is not the constraint; your ability to find and keep clients is.

What you actually charge

Three pricing models dominate, per agency-fee surveys 10-20%:

  • Percentage of ad spend — typically 10-20% of the client's monthly budget. Simple, but it punishes you for keeping budgets lean and caps you on small accounts.
  • Flat monthly retainer — commonly $500-$1,000/mo for a single-location business, scaling to $2,500-$5,000+/mo for multi-campaign accounts $500-$1,000. Best for predictable income.
  • Hybrid — a base plus a small percentage (e.g. "$750/month plus 5% of spend") $750/month plus 5%. Aligns you with growth without exposing you on tiny budgets.

Most operators also charge a one-time setup fee of $500-$2,500 $500-$2,500 to build the account from scratch — this is your fastest path to a first dollar.

Pick flat retainer + setup fee to start. It's the easiest to quote, the easiest for a small-business owner to say yes to, and it doesn't require them to disclose budgets before they trust you.

Saturation, honestly

This is a competitive space — score it high. Thousands of agencies and freelancers already do this, and the mid-market is well covered. But the saturation is uneven: national agencies ignore the plumber, the dentist, the local law firm, and the $1,500/mo restaurant because those accounts are too small for their cost structure. The opening is local + niche. Own "Google Ads for HVAC companies in Texas" rather than "Google Ads." A specialist who knows one vertical's keywords, seasonality, and cost-per-lead beats a generalist on price-to-value every time.

How to start, step by step

  • Learn the platform on your own dime. Run a real $300 campaign for yourself, a friend's business, or a fake product. Earn the free Google Ads certifications (Search, then Performance Max) through Skillshop. You cannot sell what you can't operate.
  • Pick one vertical. Choose an industry with high customer value (a closed deal worth $1k+) and clear local intent — home services, dental/medical, legal, B2B services. High ticket means the client can easily afford your fee from one extra customer.
  • Build proof. Run one account well — even at cost or free for a first client — and capture the before/after: cost per lead down, conversions up. One clean case study is worth more than any pitch deck.
  • Set your offer. Lead with a flat retainer ($750-$1,000/mo) plus a $500-$1,000 setup fee. Define exactly what's included: account build, weekly optimization, monthly report, a monthly call. Clarity closes deals.
  • Stand up the basics. A one-page site with your niche + case study, a simple monthly reporting template (Looker Studio is free), and a contract with a 90-day initial term so you have time to prove ROI before they can churn.
  • Do outreach in volume. Cold-call/email 20 businesses a day in your vertical. Lead with a free account audit ("I'll show you the 3 things wasting your budget") — this is the highest-converting opener because it gives value before asking for money.
  • Deliver the audit live. Screen-share their account (or a competitor's, using the Ad Transparency Center if they won't grant access). Point at wasted spend on broad keywords, missing negative keywords, and no conversion tracking. The gaps sell the engagement for you.
  • Land the setup fee first. Quote the one-time build before the retainer — it's an easier yes and it's your first dollar inside ~30 days.
  • Retain by reporting in their language. Owners don't care about CTR. They care about leads and revenue. Report cost-per-lead, leads, and ROI every month, on time. Retention is the whole game — your income compounds only if accounts don't churn.
  • Productize and scale. Build SOP checklists for account builds and weekly optimizations. Once you have 10-15 accounts (~$10k-$15k/mo), hire a contractor to run optimizations off your SOPs and shift yourself to sales and client relationships.

The honest risks

  • Conversion tracking is everything. If you can't prove leads, you can't prove ROI, and you'll churn. Insist on call tracking and proper tag setup before you take a client.
  • You inherit blame for Google's chaos. Algorithm shifts, Performance Max black boxes, and CPC inflation are out of your control but land on your desk. Set expectations early.
  • Budget-percentage pricing on a small account starves you. A 15% fee on a $1,500 budget is $225/mo — not a business. Use flat retainers below ~$5k of spend.
  • Churn risk is front-loaded. The first 60-90 days, before results compound, are when clients bail. The 90-day term and a strong onboarding bridge that gap.

Bottom line

The market is huge and proven, the deliverable is measured in the client's own dollars, and startup cost is near zero. The catch is that it's crowded at the top — so don't compete at the top. Go local, go niche, prove ROI in plain language, and build the retainer book that pays you while you sleep.

Gutter Cleaning Service

Gutter cleaning is one of the cleanest on-ramps into the home-services trades: low equipment cost, an obvious recurring need (leaves fall every year, twice in many climates), and a price point homeowners will pay without a second quote. You are selling the avoidance of a $5,000-$15,000 problem — water intrusion, fascia rot, foundation damage, ice dams — for a couple hundred dollars. That value gap is why margins are high and closing is easy.

The opportunity

The U.S. gutter services market was worth $795.4M in 2025 (narrow IBISWorld definition: cleaning, plus light repair and installation), and it grew 2.2% year-over-year. Demand floor is structural: there are now roughly 132.9 million U.S. households, the majority single-family homes that all have gutters needing service one to two times per year.

This is not a winner-take-all market. It is fragmented across handymen, landscapers who upsell it, and one-truck operators — which means a punctual, insured, photo-documenting operator with online booking can take share fast in any metro.

Market sizing

  • TAM: the full national gutter-services market.
  • SAM: the slice a regional residential operator can realistically reach — roughly a quarter of the national figure once you strip out other metros and the installation-heavy commercial work you won't chase early.
  • SOM: what one truck can actually book in the first year or two — a few hundred jobs on a tight route.

Saturation: 55/100. Easy to enter, crowded with casual operators, but no national brand owns it and the recurring nature rewards whoever earns the repeat. Professionalism is the moat.

The economics

  • Startup cost: $1,500 to $10,000 all-in. The low end is a ladder, a blower, a scoop, gloves, and a phone; the high end adds a used van and a gutter-vacuum system.
  • Core equipment: roughly $500-$1,000 for the initial tool setup, per ZenBusiness.
  • Insurance: budget $500-$1,000/year for liability — non-negotiable when you're working at height on someone's roof.
  • Pricing: $150-$250 per typical residential service; larger two-story homes and add-ons push higher.
  • Add-on revenue: gutter-guard installation runs $300-$800 per job and turns a one-time cleaning customer into a higher-ticket sale.
  • Income ceiling: Upper reports full-time solo operators in the $60,000-$120,000 range, with two-person teams reaching $150,000-$250,000.

Time to first dollar: ~2 weeks. The work is unskilled enough that your only real gating items are registration, insurance, and finding the first roof.

How to start (step by step)

  • Validate your micro-market. Drive your target neighborhoods. Two-story homes, mature trees, and older housing stock = the best customers. Note that wooded suburbs need two cleanings a year (spring and fall) — that's your recurring revenue engine.
  • Register the business. File a sole proprietorship or LLC with your state (registration/licensing fees run roughly $50-$500 per ZenBusiness). Get an EIN from the IRS (free). Open a separate business bank account on day one — never commingle.
  • Buy liability insurance before you touch a ladder. This is the single most important step. You are working at height. General liability protects you, and proof of coverage closes skeptical homeowners. Budget the $500-$1,000/year.
  • Buy the minimum viable kit. A quality extension ladder with stabilizer, a leaf blower (gutter attachment), a gutter scoop, a bucket/tarp, work gloves, and safety glasses. Add a corded or cordless gutter-vac later when cash flow allows — it lets you work from the ground on single-story homes and is a major safety and speed upgrade.
  • Set transparent pricing. Price per linear foot or by home size/stories. Publish a clear range so you're not negotiating on every call. Always quote downspout flushing and a debris-haul-away as included — it removes the most common objection.
  • Document everything with photos. Before-and-after shots of each gutter run are your best marketing and your defense against disputes. Text them to the customer when the job's done. This single habit separates you from the handyman and earns referrals.
  • Land the first 10 jobs by hand. Door-knock the wooded streets you scouted. Post in neighborhood Facebook groups and Nextdoor. Offer a small "first-clean" discount in exchange for a review. Your goal is reviews and a route, not margin, on these first jobs.
  • Build the recurring engine. Before you leave any job, book the next visit (or a spring/fall plan). Set calendar reminders to text past customers each season. A retained customer cleaned twice a year is worth far more than a one-off — protect and grow that list relentlessly.
  • Add the upsells. Once you have a route, layer in gutter-guard installs, roof debris removal, and pressure washing. These ride on the same truck and customer relationship and dramatically raise your average ticket.
  • Systematize and decide on growth. Get a simple booking/CRM tool, a branded truck magnet, and a Google Business Profile with your photos and reviews. From there, you choose: stay a high-margin solo, or hire a helper and run two routes during peak season.

The honest risks

  • It's seasonal. Revenue spikes in spring and fall and thins in summer/deep winter. Stack complementary services (pressure washing, snow/holiday lights) to smooth the year.
  • It's physical and dangerous. Falls from height are real. Insurance, ladder discipline, and ground-based vacuum gear for single-story work matter.
  • Low barriers cut both ways. Anyone can buy a ladder. You win on reliability, documentation, insurance, and the recurring relationship — not on being the cheapest.

HVAC Install and Repair

Heating and cooling is one of the most durable home-services businesses you can start. When a furnace dies in January or an AC quits in a July heatwave, the homeowner does not shop on price — they want someone competent on the phone today. That urgency, combined with recurring maintenance and equipment that wears out on a predictable schedule, makes HVAC a cash-generating, recession-resistant trade rather than a discretionary purchase.

Why this niche

  • The market is enormous and stable. US heating & air-conditioning contractors generated 158400000000 in 2025 revenue, and the segment has grown steadily year over year.
  • Demand for the labor is growing faster than average. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects HVAC mechanic and installer employment to grow 8 percent from 2024 to 2034, with roughly 40100 openings per year over the decade.
  • The pay floor is real. Median annual wage for the trade was 59810 in 2024 — meaning a competent owner who bills out labor at 3-4x that rate has healthy margin.
  • Equipment ages on a clock. A residential system lasts roughly 10-15 years, so a metro accumulates a steady, non-discretionary replacement pipeline that does not disappear in a downturn.

The honest downsides

This is a high-saturation trade (saturation score 72). Every metro already has a dozen established shops, national brands, and franchise operators with financing programs and fleets. You will not win on novelty — you win on answering the phone, showing up fast, clean trucks, and a wall of five-star reviews. It is also physical, seasonal (feast in summer/winter, famine in shoulder months), and capital-intensive once you add trucks and techs.

What it costs and how fast you get paid

A licensed owner-operator can launch lean for around 30000 — a used service van, core gauges/recovery/vacuum equipment, license, bond, liability insurance, and a small marketing/parts float. Buying an existing customer book costs far more but skips the cold start. Because demand is urgent and constant, the bottleneck to your first paid call is licensing and certification, not finding customers — most new operators can be invoicing within 30 days of being licensed and insured.

Step-by-step: how to start

  • Get the federal certification first. EPA Section 608 technician certification is legally required for anyone who maintains, services, repairs, or disposes of equipment containing regulated refrigerants — this is not optional under the Clean Air Act. Pursue Universal certification so you can work on all equipment types. The credential does not expire. See the EPA Section 608 page.
  • Get licensed in your state/locality. Most states require a contractor or specialty HVAC license, which typically means documented field experience, a passed exam, a contractor bond, and proof of insurance. Check your state contractor licensing board for the exact path — requirements vary widely by state.
  • Form the business and insure it. Register an LLC, get an EIN, open a business bank account, and buy general liability insurance (and workers' comp before you hire). Many municipalities also require a local business license and permits per job.
  • Build the truck. A reliable service van plus the core kit: manifold gauges, refrigerant recovery machine, vacuum pump, leak detector, combustion analyzer, multimeter, and a stocked parts bin of common capacitors, contactors, and filters.
  • Set up to get found and get paid. Create a Google Business Profile (this is your #1 lead source in home services), list on the major service directories, set up online booking and card/financing payment, and adopt field-service software for scheduling, invoicing, and follow-up.
  • Bootstrap revenue before you have a brand. Subcontract overflow from an established shop, take emergency no-heat / no-cool calls, and offer seasonal tune-up specials to fill shoulder months. Every job ends with an ask for a review and an enrollment offer for a maintenance plan.
  • Turn one-time jobs into recurring revenue. Sell annual maintenance agreements (two visits/year). They smooth out seasonality, lock in customers before competitors call, and create a predictable base of replacement leads as their equipment ages out.
  • Hire and systematize when demand outstrips you. Add a second tech and truck only when your own calendar is consistently full; standardize pricing, checklists, and a clean uniform/branding so quality survives delegation.

Where the leverage is

The operators who pull away from the pack do three boring things relentlessly: they answer the phone live (or call back within minutes), they collect and respond to reviews on every job, and they sell maintenance plans so winter and summer demand carries the slow months. Equipment and technical skill are table stakes — distribution, response time, and recurring contracts are the moat.

Sources

  • IBISWorld — Heating & Air-Conditioning Contractors in the US, Market Size
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Occupational Outlook Handbook: HVAC Mechanics and Installers
  • U.S. EPA — Section 608 Technician Certification

Handmade Candle Brand

Candles are the classic "kitchen-table to real-business" product: cheap to start, infinitely brandable, and sitting inside a home-fragrance category that keeps growing as people spend on self-care and home aesthetics. The catch is that everyone knows this, so the money is in the brand and the niche, not in the wax.

Is the market big enough?

Yes, but it is crowded. The global candle market was roughly 10.5 billion USD in 2024, projected to reach about USD 17 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 4.83 percent. The US slice alone generated revenue of about 3.4 billion USD in 2024. Container candles are the single largest format.

The flip side: barriers to entry are near zero, and Etsy alone reported around 5.6 million active sellers, with candles a perennially top home-decor category. That is why this niche scores high on saturation. You are not competing on "can I make a candle" - you are competing on scent identity, packaging, story, and distribution.

The numbers at a glance

  • TAM (global candle market): ~USD 10.5B
  • SAM (US candle market): ~USD 3.4B
  • SOM (realistic solo brand, year 1-2): ~USD 120k/yr run-rate (estimate)
  • Saturation: 78/100 (high - differentiate or die)
  • Startup cost: ~USD 1,500 home-based (range USD 500-2,000)
  • Time to first dollar: ~21 days

Where the margin actually is

A 8-9oz soy container candle costs roughly USD 3-5 in materials (wax, wick, fragrance oil, vessel, label) and retails for USD 18-30. The gross margin is excellent. What kills new brands is not COGS - it is (1) customer acquisition cost on saturated marketplaces, and (2) wasted inventory from skipping burn-testing. Fix those two and the unit economics are some of the friendliest in physical products.

How to start: step-by-step

  • Pick a sharp niche, not "candles." Crystal/intention candles, masculine scents, locally-themed scents, pet-safe, luxury minimalist, or a single signature fragrance line. A narrow niche is how a new shop beats the 5.6M-seller noise.
  • Choose your wax and lock one base recipe. Soy is the beginner default (clean burn, easy to source, "natural" marketing). Buy from a reputable supplier (e.g. CandleScience) and master ONE wax before adding coconut/beeswax blends.
  • Buy a minimal starter kit (~USD 200-500 of the budget). Wax, wicks (multiple sizes for testing), fragrance oils, a pouring pitcher, a digital scale, a thermometer, and vessels. Total home startup runs about USD 1,500 once you add branding and entity setup.
  • Burn-test relentlessly before selling anything. Pour test batches, then burn each for the full melt-pool, checking for tunneling, sooting, and scent throw (cold and hot). Wick size is the #1 thing new makers get wrong. Do not list a candle you have not burned end-to-end.
  • Nail packaging and a name. The vessel, label, and box ARE the product in a saturated market. Spend on a clean label and a memorable brand name before spending on ads.
  • Handle the legal/safety basics. Form a simple business entity, get product liability insurance, and follow ASTM candle labeling/safety warnings (warning label on the bottom is standard). This protects you when you scale into wholesale.
  • Launch on two channels at once. List on Etsy (built-in buyer traffic) AND open a simple Shopify/Square store you own. Photograph candles lit, in a styled home setting - over 70% of candle buyers want to assess fragrance/quality, so your imagery and scent descriptions do that job online.
  • Get first sales, then chase reviews. Price for healthy margin, offer a small launch discount, and ask every early buyer for a review and a photo. Reviews are the flywheel on marketplaces.
  • Reinvest into a hero SKU and local stockists. Find your best-selling scent, double down, then pitch local boutiques, coffee shops, and gift stores for wholesale - that is where indie candle brands escape marketplace fee/ad pressure.
  • Layer in repeat revenue. Add candle refills, a subscription "scent of the month," and seasonal limited drops. Repeat buyers are what turn a ~USD 120k hobby into a real brand.

Honest take

This is one of the best niches to LEARN product business cheaply, and a hard niche to get rich in by accident. The makers who win treat it like a fashion/fragrance brand (identity, drops, story) - not a craft. Start small, burn-test everything, and let one signature scent do the heavy lifting.

Holiday Light Installation

Holiday light installation is one of the cleanest seasonal home-service plays: a short, intense selling window, cash collected up front, low equipment cost, and an installable-once / remove-later structure that lets you book the same customer twice in one season. The whole business compresses into roughly October through January, which is both the appeal (a side hustle that doesn't eat your year) and the trap (miss the window and you wait twelve months).

Why this niche

  • Low startup, fast cash. You can launch for $1,940 to ~$2,700 if you don't already own a ladder and basic tools. Customers typically pay before or at install, so you're not floating receivables.
  • Two billable events per customer. Install in November, take-down and storage in January. The take-down is pure-margin recurring work most amateurs skip.
  • Premium willingness to pay. Homeowners increasingly treat professional lighting as a service, not a chore, and the average job lands around $1,000 with a sensible minimum (~$495) to keep small jobs profitable.
  • Pricing has real ceilings. Standard residential runs roughly $8-15 per linear foot, premium $15-25, and permanent/smart systems push $35-100/ft installed — the highest-margin upsell in the category.

Market size (read the labels)

The global Christmas lights and decoration market was valued at roughly $8.39B in 2025, growing ~3.75% annually. Be careful: that TAM is mostly product retail (the lights, inflatables, and decor people buy at the store), not installation labor. The SAM and SOM figures in this entry's front-matter are explicitly labeled estimates derived from that TAM — they apply a services-share assumption and a regional-capture assumption, and are not independently measured installation-revenue numbers. Treat them as order-of-magnitude framing for "is the addressable service layer big enough?" (yes), not as a forecast of your bank account.

Saturation

Saturation scores ~55/100 — moderately competitive. The low barrier means lots of part-timers flood in, but they cluster in dense affluent zip codes and bail when the weather turns. The structural gaps:

  • Suburban and mid-size metros are chronically under-served at peak; the pros concentrate where the trophy homes are.
  • Take-down and storage is left on the table by most one-season hobbyists — own it.
  • Commercial / HOA / municipal contracts ($2,500-$15,000+ per property) reward whoever shows up insured and reliable, which thins the field fast.

Startup cost

Plan for ~$1,940-$2,715+ to start, per Jobber's breakdown: business registration ($75-$400), liability insurance ($400-$700+), scheduling software (~$400), lighting inventory and clips (~$865+), a uniform, and a basic site plus cards. You can go lower if you own a ladder and a vehicle; you can go to $5,000-$30,000 if you front-load premium commercial-grade product to win bigger jobs.

Time to first dollar

Days to ~2 weeks if you start inside the season. This is a door-to-door / referral business at small scale; a single weekend of canvassing an affluent neighborhood in early November can produce paying installs the same week. Out of season, time-to-first-dollar is effectively "wait for October." The lever is timing, not skill.

How to start (step by step)

  • Pick your window and pre-sell early. Lock your service area and start booking in September-October. The customers who book early are the loyal, high-margin ones; latecomers want you on December 20 in the cold.
  • Register and insure. Form an LLC or register a sole prop, get general liability insurance (non-negotiable — you're on ladders at customers' homes), and open a business bank account.
  • Buy commercial-grade inventory, not retail. Source professional C9/LED strands, all-weather clips, timers, and extension cords. Retail big-box lights fail and burn your reputation. Buy enough for ~3-5 average homes to start and reorder as you book.
  • Set linear-foot pricing with a floor. Price at ~$8-15/ft for standard residential, set a minimum job (~$495) so small jobs don't lose money, and quote install + take-down + storage as one package.
  • Standardize the quote. Measure rooflines and trim from the curb (or via satellite measuring tools), multiply by your rate, add design/peak-accent line items. A repeatable quote is what lets you scale past yourself.
  • Canvass the right blocks. Door-knock and yard-sign affluent, single-family neighborhoods. Offer a referral discount — this category spreads almost entirely by "who did your lights?"
  • Collect up front, schedule tightly. Take deposit or full payment at booking. Batch installs by neighborhood to cut drive time during your few productive weeks.
  • Sell the take-down and storage. Book the January removal at install time. It's recurring, low-effort, and locks the customer in for next year.
  • Upsell permanent / smart systems. For repeat customers, pitch permanent track lighting ($35-100/ft installed) — far higher ticket and it converts a seasonal customer into a one-time premium install plus annual service.
  • Capture every customer for next year. Save addresses, measurements, and design notes. Year two you re-quote in minutes and your re-book rate is your whole moat.

The honest risks

  • One window, no do-overs. A slow October-November can sink the year. De-risk by pre-selling and by adding an adjacent off-season service (pressure washing, gutter cleaning) that uses the same ladders and customer list.
  • Weather and safety. You're on roofs in cold, wet conditions. Insurance and a no-ice-day policy aren't optional.
  • Cash-flow shape. Money comes in a lump and inventory is bought ahead — manage the float so a strong season doesn't become a January cash crunch.

Bottom line

If you want a low-capital business that pays in weeks and rewards organization over talent, holiday lighting is one of the best on-ramps. The winners aren't the best installers — they're the operators who pre-sell, own the take-down, and re-book last year's list before competitors knock.

Home EV Charger Installation

Every electric vehicle that gets sold creates a small, recurring electrical project: someone has to run a 240V circuit to where the car parks and mount a Level 2 charger on the wall. That's a clean, repeatable, high-margin job for a licensed electrician — and the volume keeps climbing even as the broader EV story gets noisy.

Why this niche, right now

US new-EV registrations hit 504,131 in Q3 2025 alone, with EVs at 12.6% of new light-duty sales that quarter. Most of those owners want to charge at home rather than hunt for public ports — and public infrastructure is badly behind, with only about 30 EVs per new public charging port added in the same period. That gap pushes demand straight into the residential install channel.

The global residential EV charger market sat at roughly $9.68B in 2025 and is forecast toward $39.4B by 2031. The same analysis estimates the US will need 25 million private chargers by 2030 to serve a projected ~33 million EVs. That is the long-run tailwind.

Market sizing (read the assumptions)

  • TAM — the global residential EV charger market, ~$9.68B (2025). This includes hardware; the install-labor slice is a subset.
  • SAM — the US EV charging infrastructure market, valued at ~$5.09B (2024). Residential installation labor is roughly half of that activity.
  • SOM — a single licensed operator or small regional crew realistically reaches a low single-digit share of the serviceable US install-labor pool. The metric above models ~$25M as a reachable regional ceiling, not what one van earns. A solo electrician doing 2-4 installs a week at $400-$1,800 labor each is the practical first-year reality.

The money math per job

Homeowners pay roughly $1,200-$3,000 all-in for a professionally installed Level 2 charger in 2025-2026. Of that, hardware is typically $300-$800 and your installation labor is the variable $400-$1,800 — the part you control. Panel upgrades to 200 amps add $1,500-$3,000 and are a frequent, profitable add-on. Outdoor runs add $200-$1,000 over indoor.

The incentive cliff you must understand

The federal 30C credit (Alternative Fuel Vehicle Refueling Property Credit) gives homeowners 30% of cost, up to $1,000 per port for installing a qualified charger at their primary residence. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act moved the termination date forward dramatically: equipment must be placed in service by June 30, 2026 to qualify. There is also an eligible-census-tract location requirement, so not every address qualifies.

What this means operationally: there is a demand pull-forward into the first half of 2026 as homeowners rush to beat the deadline, followed by a likely air pocket. Plan your marketing calendar and cash flow around it. Many utilities also stack their own $250-$1,200 rebates independent of the federal credit — those persist and are a strong post-cliff selling point.

What it takes to do this legally

This is licensed electrical work, not a handyman gig. In most jurisdictions you need a licensed electrician on the job and a permit. A growing number of programs and utilities require EVITP certification (Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program). To certify you must already be a licensed electrician or document at least 8,000 hours of electrical construction experience, then complete ~20 hours of training and pass the exam, at a cost of $400-$800. California, for example, requires EVITP-certified electricians on most publicly funded charging work. Treat EVITP as table stakes for credibility even where it isn't strictly mandated.

How to start (step by step)

  • Confirm your license footing. You need (or need access to) an active electrician's license in your state. If you aren't licensed, partner with a licensed electrician or pursue licensure first — this gates everything else.
  • Get EVITP-certified. Budget the ~20-hour course and $400-$800 fee. It's the single clearest trust signal to homeowners, utilities, and rebate programs.
  • Stand up the business basics. Register the entity, get general liability insurance and any required bond, and confirm your local permitting process for residential 240V circuits and service upgrades.
  • Build a tight install kit. A 240V/40-50A circuit job needs the right breakers, conduit/wire stock, a quality multimeter and clamp meter, torque tools, and a load calculator. Stock for the most common 48A hardwired and 40A plug-in installs.
  • Pick a charger stance. Decide whether you supply hardware (more revenue, more inventory risk) or install customer-supplied units (lower risk, faster). Many pros offer both and steer customers to a couple of reliable smart-charger SKUs.
  • List on installer-matching platforms. Get on the networks homeowners and automakers route leads through (e.g., Qmerit, GreenLancer, dealer/OEM install programs). These deliver your first jobs while your own marketing ramps.
  • Win the local search game. A simple site, a Google Business Profile, and reviews that mention "EVITP," "Level 2," "panel upgrade," and your metro area capture high-intent searchers.
  • Sell the whole electrical picture. The charger is the door-opener; the margin lives in panel upgrades, load management devices (to avoid a costly service upgrade), and subpanels. Quote those proactively.
  • Ride the June 2026 deadline, then pivot the pitch. Through mid-2026, lead with the expiring 30% federal credit to create urgency. After it lapses, lead with utility rebates, lower home charging cost vs. public, and convenience.
  • Systematize repeat demand. Multi-unit dwellings, small fleets, and HOAs are higher-ticket follow-ons. One clean residential install in a neighborhood often seeds several more — ask for referrals on site.

Honest risks

  • Policy whiplash. The federal credit cliff and shifting EV mandates make demand lumpy. Don't build a model that assumes the credit survives mid-2026.
  • Licensing is a real moat — both ways. It keeps amateurs out (good for you), but it also means you can't shortcut into this without the trade credential.
  • Commoditization on simple jobs. Plug-in installs on a healthy panel are quick and competitive. Differentiate on the complex work (upgrades, load management, outdoor runs) where skill and certification matter.

The durable edge here is being the licensed, EVITP-certified pro who can quote a panel upgrade and a charger in one visit — not the cheapest plug-and-mount.

Interior and Exterior Painting

Painting is one of the lowest-barrier, fastest-to-cash trades you can start. You can put a brush in your hand for a few hundred dollars and book your first paid room before you ever register an LLC. That low barrier is also the catch: nearly everyone can start, so winning is about reliability, finish quality, and how you sell — not about owning rare equipment.

Why this niche

The US house-painting-and-decorating-contractor market is worth roughly 28200000000 in 2025. Demand is steady and recurring: interior walls get repainted every 5-10 years, exteriors every 5-7, and every home sale, rental turnover, and renovation creates a fresh job. A whole-home interior repaint averages roughly 4000 to 10000, so a handful of jobs a month is real income.

It is also a forgiving business model. Materials are bought per-job (often reimbursed in the bid), there is no inventory to carry, and you can stay solo or scale to a crew on your own timeline.

Market sizing

  • TAM — 28200000000: the entire US house-painting-and-decorating-contractor industry.
  • SAM — 5640000000: the share that excludes new-construction and large commercial work, which favor big crews and general contractors.
  • SOM — 250000: a grounded year-1-to-2 revenue ceiling for one operator.

Saturation: high but beatable

The competitive picture is crowded — there are roughly 252,000 painting businesses in the US, and about 75% of them run with four or fewer people. That is why the saturation score sits at 72. Translation: you are not fighting a few giants, you are fighting hundreds of disorganized one-person shops. Beat them on the things they ignore — answering the phone, showing up on time, written quotes, clean drop-cloth work, and a follow-up text. Professionalism is the moat.

Money to start and time to first dollar

  • Startup cost: 500 solo with basic gear, up to 15000 with a sprayer, upgraded ladders, insurance, marketing, and a small crew (a work van is extra).
  • Time to first dollar: about 14 days from the moment you start asking for work.

How to start: step-by-step

  • Decide your lane. Start with interior repaints — they are weather-independent, year-round, and easier to learn than exterior prep. Add exterior, fences, and cabinets once you have reps.
  • Buy the starter kit. Quality brushes and roller frames, extension poles, drop cloths, painter's tape, a basic ladder, buckets, trays, and prep tools. This is the 500 tier. Skip the airless sprayer until a job pays for it.
  • Register and insure. Form an LLC (or start as a sole proprietor), get an EIN, and buy general liability insurance before you touch a customer's home — most homeowners and every property manager will ask. Check whether your state or city requires a contractor or painting license.
  • Nail your pricing. Price by square foot or by room, and always include prep and materials in the bid. Use the local market range (interior often $2-$6/sq ft installed) as your anchor, then quote in writing every time.
  • Get your first three jobs from people who already trust you. Post in your neighborhood and local groups, tell every contact you paint now, and offer to do a friend's room at a fair rate for photos and a review.
  • Document everything. Before-and-after photos of each job become your portfolio and your ads. Ask for a Google review the day you finish, while the customer is happy.
  • Set up a simple booking and quoting flow. A free Google Business Profile, a phone number you actually answer, and a one-page quote template will put you ahead of most competitors immediately.
  • Reinvest into speed. Once jobs are steady, buy the airless sprayer and better ladders — they cut interior and exterior time dramatically and let you bid bigger work or add a helper.
  • Build repeat and referral loops. Send a thank-you and a "remember us for your exterior next spring" message. Repeat homeowners and property managers are the path from $50k to the 250000 ceiling.

The honest downsides

It is physical, weather can stall exterior work, and slow-paying clients exist — quote in writing, take a deposit, and collect on completion. Quality complaints almost always trace back to prep you skipped to save time; do the prep and your reviews take care of marketing for you.

Junk Removal and Hauling

Junk removal is one of the lowest-barrier service businesses you can start: a truck or trailer, a strong back (or two), insurance, and a phone. People always have stuff they want gone yesterday — after a move, a renovation, a death in the family, an eviction, a hoarder cleanout, or a tenant turnover — and they will pay a premium for "you handle everything, today." That urgency is the entire business model.

Why this niche works

  • Recurring demand from non-recurring events. Moves, remodels, estate cleanouts, and property turnovers happen constantly across any metro. You are never selling to the same desperate customer twice, but the supply of desperate customers never runs out.
  • Cash-flow positive almost immediately. You get paid the day you do the work. No 60-day invoicing, no inventory, no product returns.
  • Margins are real. A well-run solo or small-crew operation commonly runs 20-30% net margins, and solo jobs can be far higher because labor is just your own time.
  • The market is large and growing. The US junk removal industry is roughly $10.2B in annual revenue, and the branded/franchise slice alone was about $2.41B in 2025 — proof that customers will pay for a trusted name, which a sharp local operator can become.

Market sizing

  • TAM (US junk removal industry): ~$10.2B/yr. This is the whole pie — every haul, every operator, nationwide.
  • SAM (branded / franchise-grade demand): ~$2.41B/yr. Customers who specifically want a professional, insured, on-time, uniformed service (i.e. not a guy with a Craigslist ad) — the segment you can actually win on quality.
  • SOM (realistic year-one capture): ~$360K/yr for a single, well-marketed truck. One truck doing ~5 jobs a day at a ~$250 average ticket, 5 days a week, is a $300K-$375K business before you ever buy truck #2.

Saturation score: 62/100 (moderately high). Low barriers mean lots of part-timers and a few national franchises crowd the easy end. But demand is fragmented by drive radius and tied to high-emotion events, so a local operator who answers the phone, shows up on time, and looks professional beats both the underpriced amateur and the slow, expensive franchise.

The economics, plainly

  • Average standard-pickup ticket: $150-$350, with a typical minimum charge of $100-$150 just to roll a truck. Full truckloads run $600-$800.
  • Startup cost: as low as $2,000 if you already own a pickup and rent a trailer; a standard launch with a used box truck, insurance, and licensing runs to about $25,000.
  • Time to first dollar: roughly 7 days if you have a vehicle. LLC, a general-liability policy, a Google Business Profile, and one local listing get you bookable inside a week.

Your two real costs per job are labor (you, plus maybe one helper) and dump/disposal fees (transfer-station tipping fees, scaled by weight). Everything else — gas, insurance, marketing — is spread across many jobs. Master the dump-vs-donate-vs-resell decision and your margins climb fast.

Step-by-step: how to start

  • Validate your radius (1 day). Search "[your city] junk removal" and list the top 5 results. Read their reviews. The complaints — no-shows, surprise pricing, slow callbacks, rude crews — are your opening. Confirm there's room and identify what you'll do better.
  • Form the legal shell (1-3 days). Register an LLC with your state's Secretary of State, get an EIN from the IRS (free), and open a business bank account. This protects your personal assets when you're hauling a stranger's heavy junk.
  • Get insured (1-2 days). General liability is the baseline (commonly a few hundred dollars a year). Add commercial auto on your hauling vehicle. Many apartment complexes and realtors — your best repeat customers — will not hire an uninsured hauler.
  • Secure your vehicle (0-7 days). Start lean: a pickup plus a rented or financed dump trailer, or a used box truck if you have capital. Don't over-buy a brand-new truck before you have demand.
  • Pull permits and find your dumps. Get any required local business license, then call your area transfer stations, landfills, scrap-metal yards, and donation centers (Habitat ReStore, Goodwill). Know each one's hours and tipping fees — this is your cost of goods sold.
  • Set transparent pricing. Price by truck-load volume (1/8, 1/4, 1/2, full) plus surcharges for heavy items (appliances, hot tubs, concrete) and stairs. Publish a minimum. Customers fear surprise pricing more than high prices — beat that fear and you win the job.
  • Build the bookable presence (1-2 days). A Google Business Profile is the single highest-ROI move — it's free and it's where "junk removal near me" searches land. Add a one-page site with photos, a phone number, and an online booking/quote form. Claim Yelp and Nextdoor.
  • Light up local lead channels. Cold-call and drop business cards with realtors, property managers, estate attorneys, and contractors — they generate cleanout jobs weekly and prize a reliable hauler. Wrap your truck (rolling billboard). Run a small Google Local Services / "Google Guaranteed" budget.
  • Do the first jobs flawlessly. Show up on time, in a clean shirt, sweep the floor when you're done, and ask for the Google review before you leave the driveway. Reviews are the flywheel — they feed your map ranking, which feeds the phone, which feeds the next review.
  • Systematize, then scale. Once you're booked solid, hire a helper, then add a second truck/crew and route them. Donate and resell the good stuff (scrap metal, working appliances, furniture) for found money on top of the haul fee.

What separates winners from also-rans

  • Answer the phone. A huge share of these jobs go to whoever picks up first. Speed of response beats price.
  • Look professional. A clean truck, a shirt, and an itemized quote let you charge franchise prices without franchise overhead.
  • Mine the relationships, not just the ads. One property manager or estate attorney can send you a steady drip of jobs for years. That's the difference between chasing every lead and having work waiting.
  • Track weight and disposal cost per job. Margins quietly bleed at the dump. Knowing your tipping fees turns guesswork pricing into real profit.

The honest downside

It's physical, it's seasonal-ish (spring/summer moving season peaks), and the low barrier means price-shoppers and amateurs are always nipping at the bottom. You manage all three by climbing upmarket — branded, insured, reviewed, and relationship-fed — where the price-shoppers can't reach you and the franchises move too slowly to compete.
