$100M Leads

Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads (Acquisition.com, 2023) answers the question that follows a good offer: now that you can sell, how do you get enough strangers to look at what you sell? The book is a field manual, not a theory. Below are the principles distilled in my own words, plus why each one matters when you are actually trying to put money in the bank.

Attribution: these ideas are Alex Hormozi's, from $100M Leads. The phrasing and the "why it matters" commentary are mine.

1. A lead is just someone you can contact — an engaged lead is the only one worth counting

Hormozi separates a "lead" (anyone you have permission to reach) from an "engaged lead" (someone who has shown they actually want what you have). Raw contact lists feel like progress but rarely convert. The whole game is moving people from the first bucket to the second.

Why it matters: Vanity metrics like followers and list size lull founders into thinking they have demand. You don't have demand until someone raises their hand. Measure engaged leads, not impressions.

2. The Core Four — there are only four ways to get leads, ever

Every lead-generation tactic collapses into 4 channels:

  • Warm outreach — contact people who already know you.
  • Post free content — broadcast value to a public audience.
  • Cold outreach — contact strangers one-to-one.
  • Paid ads — pay a platform to put you in front of strangers.

The first two cost time; the second two scale with money. Warm outreach and free content are where the broke-and-unknown should start because they require no ad budget.

Why it matters: When growth stalls, founders chase exotic "hacks." There are no other channels. If a channel isn't working, you either execute it more, execute it better, or pick a different one of the four — you don't invent a fifth.

3. Give away absurd value first — the lead magnet earns the right to sell

A lead magnet is a small, complete solution you give for free that solves one real, specific problem. It both proves you can deliver and naturally exposes the bigger problem your paid offer solves. The mistake is making a lead magnet that is useless on its own (a teaser) instead of genuinely valuable.

Why it matters: Trust is the currency before money. A free thing that actually works converts strangers into believers far cheaper than any ad creative. Generosity is a customer-acquisition strategy, not charity.

4. The Rule of 100 — beat volume before you optimize

Hormozi's prescription for someone with no traction: do 100 primary marketing actions per day for 100 days straight (100 outreach messages, or one piece of content, or $100 of ad spend, depending on the channel).

Why it matters: Most people quit before they have enough data to know whether a channel works. Volume is what generates the data. You cannot optimize a thing you have not done enough times to measure. Consistency, not cleverness, is the early-stage bottleneck.

5. Lead Getters — stop being the only one who sells

Once your own four channels work, you multiply reach through other people. Hormozi names four "Lead Getters":

  • Customers — engineer referrals so happy buyers bring more buyers.
  • Employees — train people to run your channels so output isn't capped by your hours.
  • Agencies — rent expertise and capacity you don't have yet.
  • Affiliates — partners who promote you to their audience for a cut.

Why it matters: A business where the founder is the only lead source has a hard ceiling — your calendar. Lead Getters convert linear effort into leveraged effort. This is the bridge from a busy operator to an actual company.

6. Content formula: grab interest, hold interest, satisfy interest

Free content lives or dies in that order. A great hook with no payoff burns trust; great substance no one clicks on never gets seen. Hormozi frames it as maximizing value per second of attention.

Why it matters: Attention is the raw input to every free channel. If you can't earn and keep it, paid ads just let you rent attention you can't convert anyway. Fixing content fixes the cheapest channel you have.

How to apply this, in order

  • Pick ONE of the Core Four based on what you have more of — time (warm/content) or money (cold/ads).
  • Build one genuinely useful lead magnet that solves a narrow problem completely.
  • Run the Rule of 100 on your chosen channel for 100 days before judging it.
  • Track engaged leads only — count raised hands, not reach.
  • Once a channel pays, add a second, then layer in Lead Getters to escape the founder-hours ceiling.

The throughline of the whole book: leads are a learnable, mechanical output of consistent action across a fixed set of channels — not luck, and not a mystery.

$100M Offers

Alex Hormozi's $100M Offers (2021) argues that the single highest-leverage thing most businesses can change is not their ad copy, their funnel, or their closing script — it's the offer itself. The book's promise is in its subtitle: make an offer so good people feel stupid saying no. The $100M Series it belongs to has 800000+ copies sold across titles per Hormozi's own store. Below is the framework distilled into the principles that actually move money, in my own words, with why each one matters when you're running a real business.

1. The offer beats everything downstream

Most operators try to fix conversion with better persuasion. Hormozi flips the order of leverage: a great offer to a desperate market makes mediocre marketing work; a weak offer makes great marketing irrelevant. His ranking is starving crowd first, offer strength second, persuasion skill last.

Why it matters: if you're grinding on headlines and call scripts while selling a commodity offer, you're optimizing the smallest lever. Fix the offer and the whole funnel re-rates.

2. The Value Equation — the mental model to memorize

Hormozi reduces perceived value to four variables (4 of them):

```

Dream Outcome × Perceived Likelihood of Achievement

Value = ---------------------------------------------------------

Time Delay × Effort & Sacrifice

```

You raise value by pushing the top up (bigger dream, more believable it'll happen) and the bottom down (faster, easier). The non-obvious insight: most businesses only ever try to raise the dream outcome ("get rich!") while ignoring the denominator. Slashing time-to-result and effort is usually the cheaper, more credible win.

Why it matters: it gives you a checklist for why an offer is weak. Boring offer? Probably the prospect doesn't believe it'll work for them (likelihood) or thinks it'll be slow and painful (denominator). Fix the specific variable.

3. Pick a starving crowd, not a clever product

A great offer in a dead market still dies. Hormozi's four market filters: real pain (need, not nice-to-have), purchasing power, easy to target, and growing. He points operators toward the three evergreen meta-markets — health, wealth, relationships — because the demand never expires.

Why it matters: market selection is a one-time decision that caps your ceiling forever. No amount of offer engineering rescues a shrinking, broke, unreachable audience.

4. Charge more — price is a value signal

Cutting price to win feels safe and is usually a trap. A low price signals a cheap product, attracts the worst clients, and starves you of the margin you need to over-deliver. Hormozi argues for premium, value-based pricing — set the price off the outcome's worth to the buyer, not your costs — and let the higher price itself raise perceived value and client commitment.

Why it matters: higher prices fund better fulfillment, better clients take the work seriously and get better results, and better results justify the price. It compounds. Racing to the bottom does the opposite.

5. Build the Grand Slam Offer (the assembly process)

A "Grand Slam Offer" is one so differentiated it can't be price-compared to anyone — you've made a category of one. The build:

  • Define the dream outcome — specific and time-bound.
  • List every obstacle between the prospect and that outcome.
  • Convert each obstacle into a solution ("how to ___ without ___").
  • Pick delivery vehicles for each solution and trim to the highest-value, lowest-cost-to-you items.
  • Bundle them into one package that's incomparable to anything on the market.

Why it matters: when your offer can't be compared, you escape the price war entirely. Competitors are left fighting for second place in a category you defined.

6. The four enhancers: scarcity, urgency, bonuses, guarantees

Once the core offer is strong, Hormozi stacks four amplifiers:

  • Scarcity — limit supply (total client cap, per-week intake cap, or cohort cap). Real limits create real FOMO.
  • Urgency — limit time (rolling cohorts, seasonal windows, deadlines). Deadlines are why the bulk of a launch's sales land in the final hours.
  • Bonuses — never discount the core offer; instead stack named, specific bonuses so the total perceived value dwarfs the price. Each bonus should solve a real next-objection.
  • Guarantees — reverse the risk. The bolder and more specific ("X result in Y days or your money back"), the more it removes the last reason not to buy.

Why it matters: these convert an already-good offer from "I'll think about it" to "I'd be an idiot to pass." They work because the core value is real — bolted onto a weak offer they just look gimmicky.

7. Name it so it sells itself

A good name pre-sells. Hormozi's recipe combines the avatar (who it's for), the goal, the time interval, and a container word (challenge, blueprint, intensive, accelerator). "The 6-Week Booked-Out Bakery Blueprint" tells the right person exactly what they get and when.

Why it matters: the name is the first thing the market sees. A precise, outcome-named offer qualifies the right buyer and repels the wrong one before a single sales call.

The one-line takeaway

Build the offer first. Engineer the value equation, sell it to a starving crowd, charge a premium that funds over-delivery, and wrap it in scarcity, urgency, bonuses, and a risk-reversing guarantee — so the offer is so obviously worth more than its price that saying no feels stupid.

---

Attribution: Concepts summarized in my own words from Alex Hormozi, "$100M Offers: How To Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No" (Acquisition.com, 2021). See sources for the book and framework breakdowns.

Atomic Habits

James Clear's Atomic Habits (2018) is the rare self-help book that actually earned its reach: published in 65 languages, 260 consecutive weeks on the New York Times bestseller list, and 20000000+ copies sold as of its 5-year mark (later reported past 25M). Below are the principles distilled in my own words, with why each one matters for building a business.

1. Systems beat goals

Clear's central reframe: you do not rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems. A goal is a desired outcome; a system is the repeatable process that produces outcomes whether you feel motivated or not.

Why it matters in business: "Hit $50K MRR" is a goal everyone in your category shares. The differentiator is the system underneath it — your outreach cadence, your follow-up sequence, your weekly review. Founders who obsess over the target and neglect the machine stall once willpower runs out. Build the machine; the number is a byproduct.

2. The 1% compound effect

Tiny improvements feel invisible day to day, but they compound. Clear's illustration: getting 1% better every day for a year leaves you roughly 37x better by the end (1.01^365 ≈ 37.78). The same math runs in reverse: 1% worse daily decays you toward zero.

Why it matters in business: Almost no single action moves the needle on its own — one more cold email, one more A/B test, one slightly better onboarding screen. The compounding is the whole game. The discomfort is that results lag effort, which leads directly to the next principle.

3. The plateau of latent potential

Habits often appear to make no difference until you cross a critical threshold — Clear calls the flat stretch before that breakthrough the "plateau of latent potential." His ice-cube metaphor: the room warms from 25 to 31 degrees with no visible change, then at 32 the ice finally melts. The melt came from all the prior, invisible work.

Why it matters in business: Most founders quit in the flat stretch — the "valley of disappointment" where the inputs are real but the outputs haven't surfaced yet. Content with no views, a funnel with no conversions, a product nobody's noticed. The breakthrough is usually one degree past where people give up. Knowing the plateau exists is what lets you keep depositing effort through it.

4. Identity-based habits

The most durable change is identity change, not outcome change. Instead of "I want to write a book," become "I am a writer." Clear's line — every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become. You don't need a unanimous vote, just a majority.

Why it matters in business: "I'm trying to get fit" loses to "I'm an athlete" because the second decides behavior automatically. Same for founders: "I'm a person who ships every week" or "I'm someone who talks to a customer every day" makes the habit self-reinforcing. Outcome goals expire on completion; identity persists and keeps generating the behavior.

5. The Four Laws of Behavior Change

Clear's operating system for engineering any habit, with the inversion for killing a bad one:

  • Make it obvious (cue) — design your environment so the right action is the visible default. Invert: make it invisible.
  • Make it attractive (craving) — bundle the habit with something you already want. Invert: make it unattractive.
  • Make it easy (response) — reduce friction; shrink the action to its smallest version. Invert: make it difficult.
  • Make it satisfying (reward) — give yourself an immediate signal of success. Invert: make it unsatisfying.

Why it matters in business: This isn't only self-management — it's a product and operations playbook. Want a team to log activity? Make it obvious (one button, in view) and easy (two fields, not twelve). Want customers to form a habit around your product? Make the core loop attractive and the payoff satisfying inside the first session. You are designing other people's cues, cravings, responses, and rewards whether you do it deliberately or not.

Two tools that operationalize the laws

  • Habit stacking — anchor a new habit to an existing one: "After I pour my morning coffee, I review the day's top three." It borrows the cue from a habit that's already automatic.
  • The Two-Minute Rule — scale any new habit down so it takes under two minutes to start. "Read before bed" becomes "read one page." The point is to master showing up before optimizing the size; you can't improve a habit that doesn't exist yet.

The one-line takeaway

You don't need a dramatic transformation. You need a small, repeatable system, run through the plateau, until your habits and your identity agree. The book's own commercial run — years on the bestseller list, not weeks — is itself a compounding-effect case study.

Blue Ocean Strategy

Blue Ocean Strategy is a framework from W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne, first published in 2005 and expanded in 2015. It has sold over 4000000 copies and been published in 49 languages. The core idea, restated in my own words below, is simple enough to act on this week and deep enough to reshape how you pick what to build.

The one-sentence version

Stop fighting for a bigger slice of a crowded, bloody market (a "red ocean"). Go make a new, uncontested market (a "blue ocean") where the old competition does not even apply.

The principles, in plain terms

1. Compete where there is no competition

A red ocean is an existing industry where everyone copies everyone, margins get thinner, and you win only by taking share from a rival. A blue ocean is demand you create that did not exist before. The point is not to out-execute the incumbents at their own game. It is to change the game so their advantages stop mattering.

Why it matters for your business: The hardest, most expensive fight is a head-to-head feature-and-price war against entrenched players. If you find a slice of customers nobody is serving well, you can charge more, spend less on marketing (the offer sells itself), and grow without a knife fight.

2. Value innovation: refuse the "either/or"

Conventional strategy says you must choose: be the cheap option OR be the premium option, low cost OR high differentiation. Kim and Mauborgne argue the breakthrough move is to do both at once. They call this "value innovation" - raise buyer value sharply while cutting your own cost structure, so you are not paying for differentiation with margin.

Why it matters: Doing both is what makes a blue ocean defensible. If you are merely cheaper, someone undercuts you. If you are merely fancier, someone copies the feature. When you deliver more of what people want AND cost less to operate, copying you means rebuilding your whole cost structure, which most rivals will not do.

3. The Four Actions Framework (the ERRC grid)

This is the practical tool. To rebuild what value means in your market, ask four questions about the factors your industry competes on, paraphrased here:

  • Eliminate - Which things the whole industry takes for granted could you drop entirely? (These often cost a lot and add little.)
  • Reduce - Which factors are over-served, built up far past what customers actually need?
  • Raise - Which factors should you push well above the industry norm?
  • Create - Which factors has nobody in the industry ever offered, that you could introduce?

Eliminate and Reduce strip out cost. Raise and Create deliver new value. Run together, they produce value innovation instead of a bigger, more expensive product.

Why it matters: Most founders only ever ask "what can we add?" The discipline of also asking "what can we kill?" is where the cost savings (and the focus) come from. A grid you can fill out in an afternoon forces both halves.

4. Reach beyond existing customers (noncustomers)

Red-ocean thinking obsesses over current buyers and segmenting them ever finer. Blue-ocean thinking looks at the much larger pool of people who do NOT buy in your category - because it is too expensive, too complicated, too intimidating, or too inconvenient. The biggest new demand usually hides among noncustomers, not in stealing your rival's accounts.

Why it matters: Your total addressable market is bigger than the people already raising their hands. Asking "why do most people refuse this whole category?" surfaces a market far larger than fighting over the few who already say yes.

5. Make the competition irrelevant, not beaten

The mental shift is the whole point: the goal is not to win the existing contest, it is to make the contest beside the point. You are not benchmarking against rivals. You are redrawing the boundaries of what the offering even is.

A worked example (the classic one)

Cirque du Soleil is the textbook case, and it shows the grid in action. The traditional circus competed on star performers, animal acts, and three-ring spectacle - all expensive. Cirque ELIMINATED animals and star-performer bidding wars, REDUCED the multi-ring chaos, RAISED the venue and artistic production quality, and CREATED a themed, theatrical, story-driven show aimed at adults and corporate buyers willing to pay theatre prices. They did not try to be a better circus. They built a new category between circus and theatre, and the old circus competition stopped applying. (See the official tools page for the framework and examples.)

How to apply it this week

  • Map your red ocean. List the 5 to 10 factors every player in your market competes on (price, speed, features, support, brand, etc.). Be honest about where you currently sit on each.
  • Find the noncustomers. Write down who in your space refuses to buy at all, and why. Group the reasons (too costly, too complex, too slow, too risky).
  • Run the ERRC grid. For each competing factor, decide: eliminate, reduce, raise, or create. Force at least one entry in every column - especially Eliminate.
  • Check for value innovation. Confirm your new offer both raises buyer value AND lowers your cost to deliver. If it only does one, keep iterating; you have a red-ocean tweak, not a blue ocean.
  • Draw the new value curve. Re-plot your offer on the same factors. If your shape looks identical to competitors, you have not moved. A blue ocean looks visibly different - high where they are low, absent where they pile on.
  • Test small, with noncustomers. Validate with the people who today say no. If they switch from "not interested" to "where do I buy this," you are onto a blue ocean.

The honest caveats

  • A blue ocean is not permanent. Success attracts imitators, and over time your blue ocean reddens. The framework expects you to keep creating new ones rather than defend one forever.
  • "Make competition irrelevant" is a goal, not a guarantee. Plenty of would-be blue oceans are just niches nobody wanted. Validation with real noncustomers is what separates a new market from a dead end.
  • This is a strategy lens, not a substitute for execution, distribution, or capital. It tells you what to build and for whom; it does not build it.

Bottom line

If you catch yourself competing on price and features against five other companies doing the exact same thing, you are in a red ocean. Blue Ocean Strategy says the higher-return move is usually to step sideways: cut what nobody truly values, add what nobody else offers, and aim at the people the whole industry ignores - so that "beating the competition" stops being the question you are trying to answer.

---

entries.body_html:
Built to Last

Most companies do not die because they ran out of ideas. They die because the founder was the idea, and the idea aged out. The average company on the S&P 500 now lasts only 15 years on the index, down from decades a generation ago. The lesson Jim Collins and Jerry Porras drew from studying 18 century-old "visionary" companies is the opposite of what most founders assume: durability is not a product, a market, or a charismatic CEO. It is an architecture. These are the principles, in my own words, and why each one is a hard business constraint rather than a poster on the wall.

1. Clock-building beats time-telling

A "time-teller" has the great idea, makes the great call, closes the great deal. A "clock-builder" creates a machine that keeps making great calls after the founder is asleep, on vacation, or gone. Collins's data showed visionary companies outperformed the market by roughly 15x since 1926 — and almost none of them did it on the strength of one genius founder.

Why it matters in business: Every process that lives only in your head is a single point of failure. The first real act of building something durable is converting your judgment into systems, checklists, hiring filters, and decision rules other people can run. If revenue stops the week you stop, you own a job, not a company.

2. Preserve the core, stimulate progress

The central paradox: the things that should never change (your values, your reason for existing) must be held more tightly than most founders dare, while everything else — products, strategies, org charts, even flagship lines of business — must be treated as disposable and constantly remade. Confusing the two is fatal. Companies that protect their products as if they were values get disrupted; companies that abandon their values to chase a trend lose the trust that made them worth buying from.

Why it matters: When you can clearly name what is sacred (the 5%) you earn permission to be ruthless about the other 95%. That clarity is what lets a 100-year-old company kill its best-selling product without an identity crisis.

3. Core ideology over profit-first

Visionary companies had a purpose beyond making money — and, paradoxically, made more money because of it. This is not sentiment. A genuine core ideology is a coordination tool: it tells a thousand employees how to act when no manager is in the room, which is most of the time.

Why it matters: Money is an outcome, not an organizing principle — you cannot rally a team, retain talent, or earn customer loyalty around "maximize quarterly margin." A reason for existing that survives a bad quarter is what keeps your best people from leaving during one.

4. Big Hairy Audacious Goals (BHAGs)

A BHAG is a goal so large and concrete it is almost frightening — a 10-to-30-year summit, not a quarterly target. It works because it is clear enough that everyone knows whether you hit it, and ambitious enough that it forces the company to become something new to reach it.

Why it matters: Incremental goals produce incremental companies. A goal you are confident you can hit changes nothing about how you operate; a goal that scares you reorganizes the whole business around achieving it.

5. The genius of AND, not the tyranny of OR

Mediocre companies pick: quality OR cost, vision OR execution, stability OR change. Visionary companies refuse the trade-off and engineer a way to have both. Most "obvious" trade-offs are just unsolved problems wearing a disguise.

Why it matters: Whenever you hear yourself or a leader say "we have to choose between X and Y," treat it as a signal that the real, harder design work hasn't been done yet. The durable companies are the ones that did it.

6. Cult-like cultures and home-grown leaders

Durable companies are intensely demanding about fit — you are either deeply aligned with the culture or you are clearly not a match, with little middle ground. And they overwhelmingly promote from within, so the core ideology is carried forward by people who absorbed it for decades rather than imported by an outside savior.

Why it matters: Strong culture plus internal succession is how "preserve the core" actually survives a leadership transition. Hiring a celebrity outsider CEO to "fix" a company is, in this data, more often a symptom of decline than a cure for it.

How to apply this

  • Audit your business for time-telling: list every decision only you can make, and convert one per week into a rule, checklist, or trained owner.
  • Write down your non-negotiable core (3-5 values, one purpose) and then aggressively question everything not on that list.
  • Set one BHAG with a 10-year horizon that genuinely intimidates you, and reverse-engineer this year's roadmap from it.
  • The next time a strategy decision is framed as "either/or," spend an hour trying to design the "both/and" before you accept the trade-off.

The S&P 500 tenure number is the whole argument in one statistic: building something that works is common; building something that lasts is rare, deliberate, and architectural. Collins's study is, at its heart, a blueprint for joining the second group.

---

Attribution: principles distilled in my own words from Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras, "Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies." See jimcollins.com.

Crossing the Chasm

Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (first published 1991) is the playbook for one specific, brutal moment: the gap between the customers who buy you because you're new, and the customers who buy you because you're safe. Almost every promising product that dies, dies in that gap. Here are the principles, in my own words, and why each one matters when you're actually trying to make money.

1. The adoption curve is not one market — it's five

Moore builds on the adoption lifecycle: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. The two groups that matter most are the early adopters (visionaries, roughly 13.5 percent of the market) and the early majority (pragmatists, roughly 34 percent).

Why it matters: These groups buy for opposite reasons. Visionaries buy a dream — they want an edge and will tolerate a half-built product to get it. Pragmatists buy a proven solution — they want references, completeness, and to not get fired for choosing you. If you sell to a pragmatist using a visionary's pitch, you lose. Same product, different language, different proof.

2. The chasm is a credibility gap, not a quality gap

The chasm sits between early adopters and the early majority. The trap: each group only trusts references from inside its own group. Pragmatists don't care that visionaries love you — visionaries are exactly the people they think are reckless. So your early traction generates zero trust with the people who hold the real money.

Why it matters: You can have glowing early customers, real revenue, and press, and still stall. Founders misread this stall as "we need more features" or "more marketing spend." It's neither. You haven't earned credibility with the next group on their terms. Recognizing the chasm for what it is stops you from burning cash on the wrong fix.

3. Win a beachhead before you win a war

Moore's core move, framed as a D-Day landing: don't attack the whole market. Pick one narrow, well-defined segment and dominate it completely — become the obvious, default, only-sane choice for that one type of customer. A small pond you own beats a big ocean where you're a rounding error.

Why it matters: Pragmatists buy what their peers buy. If you're 80 percent of the use in one tight niche, every prospect in that niche hears about you from someone exactly like them. Concentration manufactures the word-of-mouth credibility you can't buy. Spreading thin across many segments produces no reference base anywhere, and you stay stuck.

4. Sell the whole product, not the core product

Visionaries will assemble the missing pieces themselves — integrations, support, training, onboarding. Pragmatists won't. They want the complete, end-to-end thing that solves the problem out of the box, with the surrounding ecosystem already in place.

Why it matters: The gap between "your technology" and "a solution someone can actually deploy without a project plan" is where deals die in the mainstream. Picking a narrow beachhead is what makes a whole product affordable to build — you only have to complete the solution for one use case, not all of them.

5. The bowling alley: knock down adjacent pins

Once you own the first niche (the head pin), use that win as leverage into the next adjacent segment, then the next — each victory funding and de-risking the one after it, until you build the momentum to take the broad market. You don't leap the chasm; you bowl across it, one pin at a time.

Why it matters: It reframes "we're stuck in a small niche" as "we have a base camp." Domination compounds. Trying to skip straight to mass market is the impatience that strands most products in the chasm forever.

6. Match your playbook to your stage

Moore's later work names distinct stages — early market, bowling alley, tornado (mainstream hypergrowth), main street (maturity). What works in one stage actively hurts in another. The scrappy visionary-selling that won the early market is the wrong motion for the pragmatist mainstream.

Why it matters: Most go-to-market failures are timing failures — running last quarter's winning playbook into a market that has moved on. Knowing which stage you're in tells you which behaviors to keep and which to kill.

The one-line takeaway

Early traction lies. The customers who first love you are not evidence that the mainstream will. To cross over, pick one niche you can utterly dominate, ship the complete solution for it, earn references from people the next buyers actually trust, and expand pin by pin. Dominate a small thing before you reach for a big one.

"Crossing the Chasm" framework attributed to Geoffrey A. Moore. Concepts summarized here in my own words; read the book for the full treatment.

Deep Work

"Deep work" is Cal Newport's term for professional activity performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that pushes your cognitive capacity to its limit. Its opposite, "shallow work," is the logistical, low-skill, often-interrupted work that fills a calendar but rarely creates lasting value. The thesis is simple and uncomfortable: the ability to concentrate without interruption is becoming both rarer and more economically valuable, which makes it a near-superpower for anyone who deliberately cultivates it.

Below are the principles distilled in my own words, plus why each one matters when you're trying to build something.

The core principles (in my own words)

1. Output is a function of focus, not just hours

Newport's working heuristic is that the quality of what you produce equals the time you spend multiplied by the intensity of your focus. Two people can spend the same eight hours and ship wildly different results because one was fragmented and the other was locked in. The lever most people ignore is the intensity term. 2

Why it matters in business: You can't always buy more hours, but you can almost always raise focus intensity. For a founder, three genuinely deep hours on the one problem that moves revenue beats a ten-hour day of reactive Slack-and-email triage.

2. Fragmentation is expensive, and you pay even after the interruption ends

The hidden tax isn't the interruption itself — it's the recovery. Gloria Mark's UC Irvine field study found people take on average about 23 minutes to return to the original task after being pulled away, and they resume it the same day only about 82% of the time. 1395 81.9

Why it matters in business: A "quick" five-minute interruption can cost half an hour of real momentum. Batching shallow work and defending uninterrupted blocks isn't a luxury — it's how you reclaim hours you didn't know you were losing.

3. Attention residue is real — finish or fully park a task before switching

Sophie Leroy's research showed that when you switch tasks, part of your attention stays stuck on the previous one, and your performance on the new task suffers — especially when the prior task was left unfinished. Multitasking doesn't split your attention cleanly; it smears the old task across the new one.

Why it matters in business: Toggling between strategy, customer support, and code all morning means none of them gets your full mind. Either finish a task or write down a clear "where I left off" note so your brain can release it. Half-closed loops degrade everything that follows.

4. Boredom is a trainable muscle, and constant novelty atrophies it

If every idle moment gets filled with a feed or a notification, you train your brain to crave stimulation and to flinch from sustained effort. Deep work demands tolerating the discomfort of staying with one hard thing. Newport's counterintuitive prescription is to schedule distraction rather than schedule focus — make the default state concentration, and let novelty be the exception.

Why it matters in business: The hardest, most valuable problems (positioning, pricing, a thorny technical architecture) require sitting in discomfort without bailing to something easier. If you can't be bored, you can't think deeply.

5. Shallow work is necessary but must be ruthlessly bounded

Email, meetings, and admin won't disappear, and pretending they will is naive. The move is to put a hard ceiling on them: a fixed budget, batched windows, and an honest audit of which "urgent" tasks actually deserve your best cognitive hours. Newport calls this "draining the shallows."

Why it matters in business: Most calendars are colonized by other people's priorities. Deciding in advance how much of your week shallow work is allowed to consume is how you keep the deep, value-creating work from being the thing that always gets squeezed out.

How to actually start

  • Audit one week honestly. Track when you do focused work versus reactive work. Most people overestimate their deep hours dramatically.
  • Schedule deep-work blocks first. Put 60–120 minute focus blocks on the calendar before meetings can claim the day. Protect them like client commitments.
  • Make distraction harder than focus. Phone in another room, notifications off, a single browser tab. Raise the friction on the easy escape.
  • Batch the shallows. Designate one or two windows a day for email and messages. Communicate the cadence so people stop expecting instant replies.
  • Close your loops. Before switching tasks, finish it or write a one-line note on exactly where you stopped, so attention residue doesn't follow you.
  • Build the boredom tolerance. Resist filling every gap with your phone. Treating waiting moments as rest, not stimulation, slowly rebuilds the capacity to concentrate.

The takeaway

Deep work isn't about grinding more hours. It's about protecting the conditions under which your best thinking happens, then defending those conditions against a world engineered to fragment your attention. In a market where almost everyone is distracted, the person who can reliably concentrate has a structural edge.

Principles attributed to Cal Newport's "Deep Work" (2016); supporting findings from Gloria Mark (UC Irvine) and Sophie Leroy. All framing and commentary above is original.

Extreme Ownership

Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win was written by Jocko Willink and Leif Babin, two highly decorated SEAL officers from the Battle of Ramadi in the Iraq War, and first published in 2015 by St. Martin's Press. It became a #1 New York Times bestseller and is now standard reading inside many companies' leadership programs. The framework is military in origin but its real subject is accountability under pressure — which makes it directly useful for anyone running a business.

These are the core ideas in my own words, and why each one earns its keep in an operating business.

1. Own everything — there is nobody else to blame

The central claim: a leader is responsible for everything in their world. Not most things. Everything. When a team misses a deadline, ships a defect, or loses a customer, the leader's first move is to look inward — what did I fail to make clear, fail to resource, fail to check?

Why it matters in business: Blame is a dead end. It feels like progress (you "found the cause") but it changes nothing, because you cannot fix a person you have decided is the problem. Owning the failure is the only stance that hands you a lever. If the result is yours, the fix is also yours.

2. There are no bad teams, only bad leaders

Willink and Babin argue that the same group of people will perform brilliantly or terribly depending almost entirely on the standard their leader sets and holds. A "weak team" is usually a team that has never been given clear expectations and consistent accountability.

Why it matters in business: Before you fire, restructure, or "find better people," ask whether the people you have were ever given a real chance — clear goals, a clear standard, and a leader who enforces it without exception. The standard you walk past is the standard you accept.

3. Believe — you can't sell what you don't buy

A leader has to genuinely believe in the mission and the plan, because conviction is contagious and so is doubt. If you don't understand why an order or strategy makes sense, your job is to go get that understanding — to push back up the chain until it's clear — not to relay a directive you can't stand behind.

Why it matters in business: Teams read their leader's real conviction, not the slide deck. A founder who privately doubts the roadmap will leak that doubt into every standup. Earn your own belief first; only then can you ask others for theirs.

4. Check the ego

Ego clouds judgment, blocks honest feedback, and makes "I was wrong" nearly impossible to say. The strongest leaders in the book are the ones humble enough to take ownership publicly and credit their people for wins.

Why it matters in business: Ego is expensive. It defends bad decisions long after the data has turned, and it punishes the messengers who bring bad news — guaranteeing you get less of the truth exactly when you need more of it.

The Four Laws of Combat

The book distills team execution into 4 operating principles:

  • Cover and Move — teams support each other; departments are not rival tribes. Every unit exists to advance the same mission, so silos that compete instead of cover are a leadership failure.
  • Simple — plans and communication must be simple enough that everyone understands them under stress. Complexity is where execution goes to die.
  • Prioritize and Execute — when everything is on fire, you cannot do everything at once. Name the single highest priority, attack it, then move to the next. "Relax, look around, make a call."
  • Decentralized Command — push decision-making down. Leaders cannot run every detail, so they communicate intent (the end state and the why) and let frontline people decide how. A practical span: roughly four to six direct sub-leaders per leader.

Why this matters in business: Most operational failures aren't strategy failures — they're execution failures caused by cross-team friction, plans nobody understood, scattered focus, or bottlenecked decisions. These four laws map almost one-to-one onto how a startup actually breaks.

5. Discipline equals freedom

The book's most quoted line is a paradox: discipline — fixed routines, standards, and self-control — is what creates freedom. Disciplined systems run without constant supervision, which frees the leader to think, and disciplined emotional control keeps you calm enough to make good calls in chaos.

Why it matters in business: The founder who builds disciplined processes (checklists, cadences, defined ownership) eventually gets to step out of the daily firefight. The one who runs on improvisation stays trapped inside it. Structure isn't the opposite of agility — it's the prerequisite for it.

Apply it this week

  • After the next miss, write the one-line version that starts with "I" — what you failed to set up — before assigning any external cause.
  • Pick one underperforming area and ask: has the standard ever actually been made explicit and enforced? Fix that before judging the people.
  • Take your current "everything is urgent" list and force-rank it. Work the top item only until it's resolved.
  • For one recurring decision, write a one-sentence "intent" and delegate the how entirely to the person closest to the work.
Attribution: principles drawn from Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win by Jocko Willink and Leif Babin (St. Martin's Press, 2015). The summary and commentary above are written in our own words for Black Label Academy; read the book for the full combat narratives behind each lesson.

Good to Great

Jim Collins' research team screened 1435 companies to find the handful that flipped from merely good results to sustained great results. Only 11 cleared the bar: a transition point after which they beat the general market by 6.9 over the next 15 years. The value of the book isn't the company list (several later stumbled) — it's the pattern of behavior that produced the leap. Here are the principles in my own words and why each one matters when you're actually building something.

1. Level 5 Leadership: ambition for the work, not the ego

The leaders who drove these leaps were not the chest-thumping celebrity CEOs. They were quiet, almost self-effacing people who poured their ambition into the company instead of their own reputation. The paradox Collins names is personal humility plus ferocious professional will.

Why it matters in business: A founder who needs to be the hero builds a company that collapses the moment they leave. A Level 5 leader gives credit outward and takes blame inward, which is exactly what makes good people stay and bad results get fixed instead of hidden. Practically: the goal is a company that outperforms after you, not a stage for you.

2. First Who, Then What: get the right people on the bus

The great companies got the right people in the right seats — and the wrong people off the bus — before they figured out where to drive. Strategy came second. The logic: if you have the right people, you don't need to over-manage or over-motivate them, and you can change direction without re-staffing.

Why it matters: Most early-stage failure is a people-quality problem disguised as a strategy problem. Hire slow on character and capability, and be honest fast when someone is in the wrong seat. A B-player in a key seat is a tax you pay every single day.

3. Confront the Brutal Facts (the Stockdale Paradox)

Great companies held two things at once: unwavering faith they would prevail in the end, and the discipline to face the most brutal facts of their current reality. Collins named it after Admiral Stockdale, who survived years as a POW — the prisoners who died were the optimists who kept setting dates that didn't come true.

Why it matters: Hope is not a plan, and denial is fatal. Build a culture where bad news travels up fast and unfiltered — lead with questions, run blameless autopsies, and make it safe to say "this isn't working." You cannot fix a reality you refuse to look at.

4. The Hedgehog Concept: do one thing better than anyone

Borrowed from Isaiah Berlin's essay — the fox knows many things, the hedgehog knows one big thing. The great companies found the single intersection of three circles: what they can be the best in the world at, what drives their economic engine, and what they are deeply passionate about. Then they killed everything outside that intersection.

Why it matters: Spreading thin is the default failure mode of ambitious people. The discipline is in what you say no to. If a new business, acquisition, or feature does not sit inside your three circles, you don't do it — even when it looks tempting.

5. A Culture of Discipline

When you have disciplined people, you don't need hierarchy. When you have disciplined thought, you don't need bureaucracy. When you have disciplined action, you don't need excessive controls. Discipline is freedom inside a clear framework — not rigid command-and-control.

Why it matters: Bureaucracy is usually a scar tissue companies grow to compensate for the wrong people. Hire self-disciplined people who fanatically own results, give them a clear frame, and get out of the way. The famous test: build a "stop doing" list, not just a to-do list.

6. The Flywheel: momentum over the big push

No transformation happened in one dramatic move. It looked, from outside, like a sudden breakthrough; from inside it was years of consistent pushes on the same heavy flywheel, each turn slightly easier than the last, until momentum took over. The opposite is the "doom loop" — lurching from initiative to initiative, never letting any one of them compound.

Why it matters: There is no silver-bullet launch. Pick the right direction, then push the same flywheel relentlessly. Consistency compounds; the search for a magic moment resets your momentum to zero every time.

How to apply this

  • Audit your bus first. Before the next strategy debate, list every key seat and rate who is in it. Fix the seats before the map.
  • Write your three circles. One sentence each: best-at, economic engine, deep passion. The intersection is your Hedgehog. Everything outside it goes on a stop-doing list.
  • Install a brutal-facts ritual. A standing, blameless review where the worst number on the dashboard gets discussed first.
  • Name your flywheel. Define the handful of repeatable moves that compound, and commit to pushing them for years — not weeks.

The throughline is unglamorous: humble leadership, the right people, honesty about reality, ruthless focus, disciplined execution, and patient compounding. None of it is a hack. That's the point.

---

Attribution: principles drawn from Jim Collins, "Good to Great: Why Some Companies Make the Leap... and Others Don't" (2001). Summary and commentary above are original; see jimcollins.com for the author's own treatment.

High Output Management

Andy Grove ran Intel through the brutal transition from memory chips to microprocessors. In 1983 he wrote down how he actually managed, and the book has outlived almost every other management text because it treats management as an engineering problem, not a personality contest. These are the principles in my own words, and why each one earns its keep in a real business.

1. A manager's output is the team's output, not their own

Grove's central equation: a manager's output equals the output of their own organization plus the output of the neighboring organizations they influence. You are not paid for the work you personally do. You are paid for what your team and the teams around you produce.

Why it matters in business: the most expensive mistake a new founder-operator makes is staying the best individual contributor. Every hour you spend doing the work yourself is an hour not spent multiplying ten other people. If your output is just your own two hands, you are an employee with a title, not a manager.

2. Find the high-leverage activities and ignore almost everything else

Leverage is output divided by the time spent producing it. A small action with large downstream impact is high leverage; busywork is low leverage. Grove flags three repeatable high-leverage moves: gathering information, making decisions that unblock many people, and "nudging" people toward the right path. Training your team and motivating them are among the highest-leverage things you can ever do, because the payoff compounds for years.

Why it matters in business: the art is selecting one, two, or three high-leverage activities and deliberately neglecting the rest. The flip side is negative leverage, just as powerful in the wrong direction: a delayed decision, meddling in work you delegated, abdicating instead of supervising, or an interruption at the wrong moment can wipe out a whole team's week.

3. Manage by indicators, and pair every one

Run your function the way a factory runs a line: with a small dashboard of indicators you check daily, not a quarterly report you read after the damage is done. Grove's twist is to pair indicators so they police each other. Measure volume and quality. Measure speed and error rate. A single metric always gets gamed; a paired one cannot be gamed without the partner metric exposing it.

Why it matters in business: "leads booked" with no "leads that showed up" produces a sales team optimizing for garbage. Pair the count with the conversion and the incentive self-corrects.

4. Catch problems while they are still cheap

The earlier in a process you detect a defect, the less it costs to fix. Grove built quality checks into each stage rather than inspecting only at the end. Inspect inputs, monitor the process, and check outputs, and do the catching at the lowest-value stage you can.

Why it matters in business: a wrong assumption caught in a one-page spec costs an afternoon. The same wrong assumption shipped to customers costs a recall, refunds, and reputation. Push your detection upstream where the value at risk is smallest.

5. Task-Relevant Maturity decides your management style

There is no single right way to manage a person. The correct style depends on their Task-Relevant Maturity (TRM): how much experience that specific person has with the specific task in front of them. Low TRM needs close, structured, hands-on direction. High TRM needs delegation, communication, and emotional support. The same star employee can be high-TRM on a familiar task and low-TRM the moment you hand them something new.

Why it matters in business: micromanaging a veteran insults them and wastes your time; turning a novice loose with "figure it out" guarantees a fire. Match the leash to the task, not to the person's title or your general opinion of them. See once a week one-on-ones for inexperienced reports and roughly monthly for veterans.

6. The one-on-one belongs to your report

Grove treated the 1:1 as the highest-leverage scheduled meeting a manager has. The cadence scales inversely with TRM: frequent for the inexperienced, sparse for the seasoned. Critically, the meeting is the report's meeting, not yours. Make them explain the situation. The more they articulate the "why" behind their choices, the faster you read their real TRM and the more they own the outcome.

Why it matters in business: a single well-run 1:1 can redirect weeks of a person's work. That is the definition of leverage, and it is nearly free.

7. Set objectives that pace themselves: the OKR seed

Grove adapted Drucker's Management by Objectives into what he called "iMBOs" at Intel around 1971. The system answers two questions: where do I want to go (the objective), and how do I pace myself to know I am getting there (the key results). John Doerr learned it inside Intel, renamed it OKRs, and later carried it to Google, where it became the goal-setting standard for modern technology companies.

Why it matters in business: an ambition with no measurable checkpoints is a wish. OKRs force you to convert "grow revenue" into a number you can fail at, which is the only kind of goal that actually changes behavior.

How to apply it this week

  • Write your manager's-output equation: list the teams whose output you are actually responsible for, and stop counting your solo work as your contribution.
  • Identify your top three high-leverage activities and put them on your calendar before anything else fills it.
  • Pick one metric you currently track and pair it with a quality or conversion partner.
  • Rate each direct report's TRM on their current main task, then set their 1:1 cadence to match.
  • Write one objective with two to three measurable key results for the next 90 days.

Attribution

These principles are distilled in my own words from High Output Management by Andrew S. Grove (Intel CEO, 1983). The book itself is the primary source; the sourced summaries above corroborate the specific figures and the OKR lineage. Read the original, it is short and dense.

How to Win Friends and Influence People

Dale Carnegie published How to Win Friends and Influence People in 1936. It has since sold more than 30000000 copies worldwide, still moves roughly 250000 copies a year, and sits at number 19 on Time's list of the 100 most influential nonfiction books. Ninety years on, it is still the operating manual for the part of business that no spreadsheet captures: how to make another human being want to work with you.

Below are the core ideas distilled in my own words, organized the way Carnegie organized the book, with a note on why each one matters when you are trying to build a company, close a deal, or lead a team.

Part 1 — How you handle people

Skip the criticism. People almost never respond to being told they are wrong; they get defensive and dig in. Condemnation feels productive but it just buys you resentment. Why it matters in business: a co-founder, vendor, or report who feels attacked stops bringing you bad news early — and bad news you hear late is what actually kills companies.

Give honest, specific appreciation. Not flattery (which is cheap and obvious), but real recognition of something real. Why it matters: attention is the cheapest retention tool you have. The employee who feels seen does not start updating their resume.

Arouse in the other person an eager want. Stop talking about what you need and start framing things around what they want. Why it matters: this is the whole of selling. Nobody buys your product because you need revenue; they buy because it solves their problem. Lead with their problem.

Part 2 — How to make people like you

  • Be genuinely interested in other people. You make more allies in a month by being interested in others than in a year of trying to make others interested in you.
  • Smile. It costs nothing and it changes the temperature of a room — and now, of a video call.
  • Use a person's name. A name is, to its owner, the most important word in any language. In a cold-outreach world, getting it right (and using it) is a free differentiator.
  • Be a good listener. Ask questions and let them talk. The person you let talk the most usually walks away thinking the conversation went great.
  • Talk in terms of the other person's interests. Do the homework. Walk into the meeting already knowing what they care about.
  • Make the other person feel important — sincerely. This is the through-line of the whole book.

Why this part matters: every deal, hire, and partnership runs on whether the other side likes dealing with you. Likeability is not fluff; it is the lubricant on every transaction you will ever do.

Part 3 — How to win people to your way of thinking

The headline lesson: you cannot win an argument. Even when you "win," you lose, because you have made the other person feel small and they will resent you for it. Carnegie's alternatives:

  • Show respect for the other person's opinion; never say "you're wrong."
  • If you are wrong, admit it fast and emphatically — it disarms people instantly.
  • Begin in a friendly way; start from agreement, not the dispute.
  • Get the other person saying "yes" early and often.
  • Let the other person do most of the talking, and let them feel the idea is theirs.
  • Try honestly to see things from their point of view, and appeal to nobler motives.

Why it matters: negotiation, fundraising, and getting a stubborn engineer to adopt your approach are all the same skill — moving someone to your position without making them feel defeated. The founder who has to be right in every meeting loses the people they most need.

Part 4 — How to lead without breeding resentment

When you have to correct someone:

  • Begin with honest praise before the criticism.
  • Call attention to mistakes indirectly, and mention your own mistakes first.
  • Ask questions instead of giving orders.
  • Let the other person save face.
  • Praise every improvement, even small ones.
  • Give people a good reputation to live up to — tell someone they are reliable and they tend to become it.

Why it matters: this is management in one page. Your job as a leader is to change behavior without burning the relationship, because you have to keep working with that person tomorrow.

The one principle under all of them

If you strip the book to a single idea, it is this: act from a sincere sense of the other person's importance, not as a manipulation tactic. Carnegie is explicit that the techniques are worthless — and quickly seen through — if they are insincere. In a business context the takeaway is durable: people remember how you made them feel long after they forget the terms of the deal, and that memory is what brings them back, refers you, and answers your next email.

How to actually apply this

  • Pick one principle a week. Do not try to install all of them at once. Run "ask questions instead of giving orders" for seven days and watch what changes.
  • Prep the other side's interests before every important conversation. Two minutes of research on what they care about beats any clever pitch.
  • Replace your next critical email with a question. "What if we tried X?" instead of "X is wrong."
  • Use names and write down details. Keep a running note on key relationships — what they care about, what you last discussed.
  • Audit your last lost deal or conflict. Which principle did you violate? Usually it is "I had to win the argument."

---

Attribution: principles distilled from Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936). Summaries above are paraphrased in original words for educational use, not reproduced from the text.

Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion

Robert Cialdini spent years undercover inside sales lots, fundraising boiler rooms, and recruiter offices to find out why people say yes. The result, first published in 1984, became one of the most-cited business books ever written: his books have sold more than 7000000 copies across 49 languages. The whole framework collapses into seven shortcuts the human brain uses to decide fast. Below is each one distilled in my own words, plus why it actually moves money in a business.

The seven principles, in plain terms

1. Reciprocity

People feel a debt the moment you give them something first. The give doesn't have to be expensive, it has to be first, unexpected, and personalized. Why it matters in business: a genuinely useful free audit, sample, or piece of advice opens a door that a cold pitch never will. The mint on the restaurant check raises tips. The free trial that already solved a real problem makes the paid plan feel like settling a debt, not taking a risk.

2. Commitment and Consistency

Once someone says yes to something small and visible, they work hard to stay consistent with it. We hate contradicting our own past statements. Why it matters: get the low-friction yes first (a newsletter signup, a 10-minute call, a one-line written goal) before you ask for the real commitment. Written and public commitments stick harder than private ones, which is why "reply YES to confirm" outperforms a silent assumption.

3. Social Proof

When people are unsure, they copy what similar others are doing. The closer the reference group is to them, the stronger the pull. Why it matters: testimonials from people who look like the prospect beat generic five-star averages. "Used by 200 roofing contractors in Texas" persuades a Texas roofer far more than "trusted worldwide." Show the herd they actually belong to.

4. Authority

We defer to credible experts, and we read credibility from signals: titles, credentials, track record, even attire and confident specifics. Why it matters: lead with the proof of expertise before the ask, not buried in an "About" page. Cialdini's own research found that having a receptionist mention a staffer's real qualifications before transferring a call measurably increased appointments. Borrowed authority (a credible third party vouching for you) lands harder than self-praise.

5. Liking

We say yes to people we like, and we like people who are similar to us, who pay us genuine compliments, and who cooperate toward shared goals. Why it matters: rapport is not fluff, it is a conversion variable. Find the real common ground, name what you genuinely admire about the prospect's business, and frame the deal as the two of you working the same problem rather than opposite sides of a table.

6. Scarcity

People want what is rare, and they fear loss more than they desire an equal gain. A genuinely limited supply, deadline, or exclusive access raises perceived value. Why it matters: real deadlines and real caps ("3 onboarding slots left this month") drive action. The critical word is real. Fake countdown timers train customers to distrust you, which poisons every other principle on this list.

7. Unity

The newest principle, which Cialdini described as hiding in his data for decades and now treats as a distinct seventh lever. Unity goes beyond mere similarity to shared identity, the sense of "one of us": family, region, tribe, alma mater, profession. Why it matters: the strongest persuasion isn't "people like you do this," it's "we do this." Build a brand people feel they belong inside, use co-creation ("we built this with you"), and speak in the in-group's language. Belonging converts where comparison only nudges.

How to actually use this without becoming a manipulator

Cialdini draws a hard line between persuasion and trickery, and so should anyone building a real business. The principles describe how trust-based shortcuts work; they only compound over time if the underlying claim is true.

  • Audit your offer against all seven. Where is the unexpected give (reciprocity)? The small first yes (consistency)? The proof from similar buyers (social proof)? The visible credentials (authority)? The genuine rapport (liking)? The real constraint (scarcity)? The shared identity (unity)?
  • Fix the weakest one first. Most offers over-index on one principle (usually scarcity or social proof) and ignore four others. The cheapest conversion gains live in the principles you're not using yet.
  • Never fake the input. A fabricated review, a fake deadline, or a borrowed credential you don't have will out-perform for one cycle and then detonate your reputation. The principles amplify whatever is real, including dishonesty.
  • Stack ethically, in order. Open with reciprocity and liking to earn the right to be heard, establish authority and social proof to de-risk, secure a small consistency commitment, then close with real scarcity, all inside a brand the buyer feels part of (unity).

The one-line takeaway

Persuasion isn't about pressure, it's about removing the reasons a good decision feels risky. Cialdini's seven principles are the seven risks the brain is scanning for. Answer all seven honestly and the yes takes care of itself.

Made to Stick

Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die by Chip Heath and Dan Heath, published in 2007, asks a brutally practical question: why do some ideas (urban legends, conspiracy theories, proverbs) lodge themselves in memory forever while carefully crafted business pitches evaporate the moment the meeting ends? The book hit the New York Times and Wall Street Journal bestseller lists and held a 24-month run on BusinessWeek's list, and it has been translated into 30+ languages. For anyone selling a product, raising money, or trying to get a team to act, it is a field manual for making a message refuse to die.

The core insight: stickiness is not a gift of charisma. It is a checklist of six traits, and the absence of any one of them is usually why your message bounces off people. The acronym is SUCCESs.

The six principles, in my own words

1. Simple — find the one thing

Strip the idea to its absolute core. Not "dumbed down" — prioritized. If you say three things, you've said nothing, because the listener can't tell which one matters. Southwest's "THE low-fare airline" is a decision filter, not a slogan: it tells a frontline employee whether to add chicken Caesar salad to a flight (no — it doesn't keep fares lowest). A great simple idea is a compact proverb that travels intact.

Why it matters in business: Your customer, investor, or new hire has a 5-second attention budget. The thing you cut is the thing that lets the one thing through. If you can't say your value in a sentence, you don't have a positioning problem — you have a clarity problem you're outsourcing to the buyer.

2. Unexpected — break a pattern, then open a gap

Surprise buys attention; the gap keeps it. First, violate the listener's expectation so their guessing machine fails and they re-engage. Then point at a hole in their knowledge — the "curiosity gap" — so they need the answer. Don't open with the answer; open with the question they didn't know they had.

Why it matters in business: Ad spend buys impressions, not attention. A surprising claim ("we will be your slowest-growing vendor") stops the scroll; the gap ("here's why that's good for you") earns the read. Lead with tension, resolve it with your product.

3. Concrete — make it sensory

Abstraction is the language of experts and the death of memory. "World-class customer service" is a fog. "We answer every call by the third ring, by a human, no phone tree" is a picture. Concrete means describable in terms of human senses and actions. Concrete details also coordinate a team: everyone hears the same instruction.

Why it matters in business: Vague promises can't be verified, sold, or delivered against. Concrete claims build trust because they're falsifiable, and they're easier for a happy customer to repeat to the next one.

4. Credible — let them test it

Make the idea believable without requiring blind faith. Use authorities — or better, anti-authorities (a smoker who got cancer beats a doctor). Use vivid statistics scaled to human experience. Best of all, use a "testable credential": invite the audience to check for themselves ("Are you better off than you were four years ago?"). Self-verification beats any claim you make about yourself.

Why it matters in business: Buyers have heard every superlative. A free trial, a public metric, a side-by-side they can run themselves — these transfer belief in a way testimonials can't. Let the product carry the credibility.

5. Emotional — make them feel, not just understand

People give to one starving child, not to statistics about millions — analysis actually suppresses the emotional response. To make people care, tap identity ("what would someone like me do?") and concrete benefit to a specific person, not abstract aggregate good. Appeal to self-interest, but also to who they want to be.

Why it matters in business: Decisions are emotional and justified with logic after the fact. A spec sheet informs; a vivid before/after of one real customer moves the purchase. Sell the transformation of a person, not the feature.

6. Stories — give them a flight simulator

A story is rehearsal. Hearing how someone solved a problem mentally simulates the action, so the listener is primed to act when reality hits. The Heaths name three useful plots: the Challenge plot (underdog/willpower), the Connection plot (bridging a divide), and the Creativity plot (the breakthrough). You usually don't have to invent stories — you have to spot the ones already around you.

Why it matters in business: Case studies, founding stories, and customer narratives outperform feature lists because they're portable and they pre-load the buyer to use the product. A sales rep armed with one great story beats a deck of bullet points.

The villain: the Curse of Knowledge

The single reason experts communicate badly is that once you know something, you can't un-know it, and you forget what it's like not to know. You speak in abstractions because they're efficient for you. Founders, engineers, and specialists are the worst offenders. SUCCESs is essentially a set of forcing functions to drag you out of your own head and back into the listener's.

Why it matters in business: Your team's deepest expertise is exactly what makes your messaging unintelligible to customers. The fix is not "talk more" — it's translation: simple, concrete, story-shaped.

How to apply it this week

  • Pressure-test your pitch: Write your core message in one sentence (Simple). If it has three ideas, you have three pitches and zero.
  • Run the SUCCESs checklist on your homepage: Which of the six is missing? Most landing pages have zero stories and zero concrete proof. Add one of each.
  • Replace one statistic with one person: In your next deck, swap an aggregate number for a single named customer's before/after (Emotional + Concrete).
  • Hunt, don't invent, stories: Ask your support or sales team for the last customer who got a surprising result. That's your next ad.
  • Add a testable credential: Give the buyer something to verify themselves — a free tier, a public dashboard, a live demo (Credible).

Attribution

Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die by Chip Heath and Dan Heath (Random House, 2007). The SUCCESs framework, the "Curse of Knowledge," and the supporting examples are theirs; the summary, commentary, and business applications above are my own paraphrase and analysis. Read the original for the full case studies and the detailed how-to.

Never Split the Difference

Chris Voss spent 24 years as an FBI hostage negotiator, rising to lead international kidnapping negotiator. Never Split the Difference, written with Tahl Raz and published by Harper Business in 2016, takes the playbook he used when lives were on the line and rebuilds it for the negotiations you actually face: salary, pricing, vendor terms, an angry customer, a co-founder split.

The title is the thesis. The classic "meet in the middle" feels fair, but Voss argues it's usually a lazy outcome that leaves value on the table and satisfies no one. Splitting the difference is what you do when you've stopped trying to understand the other side. Below are the principles in my own words and, more importantly, why each one earns its place in business.

1. Tactical empathy: feel it, don't fold

Empathy in Voss's sense is not being nice and it is not agreeing. It is the deliberate act of identifying the other person's emotional state and the reasons behind it, then naming it back to them so they feel understood. You can have complete tactical empathy for a counterpart you intend to out-negotiate.

Why it matters in business: People do not make decisions on spreadsheets alone; they decide emotionally and justify logically. A buyer who feels understood lowers their guard and tells you what actually drives the deal. You cannot solve for a constraint the other side never voices.

2. Mirroring: repeat the last few words

When someone finishes a thought, calmly repeat their final one-to-3 words back as a question. "We can't move on the timeline." — "The timeline?" It feels almost too simple, but it triggers the other person to expand, clarify, and often talk themselves into giving you more.

Why it matters in business: It is the cheapest information-gathering tool you have. On a sales or vendor call, mirroring keeps them talking while you say almost nothing — and whoever is talking is revealing their position.

3. Labeling: name the emotion to defuse it

A label is a sentence that begins with "It seems like…", "It sounds like…", or "It looks like…" and then states the emotion you observe. "It seems like you're worried this won't be delivered on time." Naming a negative emotion drains its intensity; naming a positive one reinforces it.

Why it matters in business: Unspoken objections kill deals silently. Labeling drags the objection into the open where you can address it, and it signals you are paying attention rather than just waiting to pitch.

4. The accusation audit: say the worst thing first

Before a hard conversation, list every brutal thing the other side could think about you or your offer, then say those things out loud before they can. "You're probably going to think this price is too high, and that we're just another agency overpromising." Voiced by you, the accusations sound exaggerated, and the counterpart instinctively pushes back toward the opposite.

Why it matters in business: It inoculates the deal. You neutralize objections preemptively and earn trust, because nobody expects the seller to name their own weaknesses.

5. Get to "That's right," not "You're right"

The goal of a summary is to make the other person say "That's right" — a sign they feel fully understood. "You're right" is a polite brush-off that ends the conversation without changing anything. Reaching "that's right" usually means you delivered a tight summary of their world, often via a label plus a paraphrase.

Why it matters in business: "That's right" is the inflection point where resistance turns into collaboration. It is the signal that you have earned the right to propose a solution.

6. "No" is the start, not the end

Voss inverts the sales obsession with getting people to say "yes." "Yes" is often a counterfeit commitment people give to make you go away. "No" makes the other side feel safe and in control, so design questions they can comfortably answer with it: "Is now a bad time to talk?" or "Have you given up on this project?"

Why it matters in business: A protected "no" surfaces real objections and gives the counterpart agency, which paradoxically makes them more cooperative than chasing a hollow "yes."

7. Calibrated questions: hand them the problem

These are open questions starting with "how" or "what" that have no fixed answer and quietly force the other side to solve your problem for you. "How am I supposed to do that?" puts the squeeze on a low offer without a confrontation. Prep 5 of them before any real negotiation. Avoid "why" — it sounds like an accusation.

Why it matters in business: Calibrated questions let you say "no" without the word, redirect aggression into problem-solving, and make the counterpart feel ownership of the outcome.

8. The Ackerman model: anchor and concede on a curve

When it's time to talk numbers, Voss teaches a deliberate haircut sequence. Set your target, open at 65 percent of it, then raise in shrinking increments — to 85, 95, and finally 100 percent — ending on a precise, odd number rather than a round one. The decreasing concessions signal you're nearing your limit.

Why it matters in business: It replaces gut-feel haggling with a disciplined structure, anchors the range in your favor, and uses the pattern of your concessions to convince the other side they've squeezed you dry.

How to apply it this week

  • Before your next negotiation, write a short accusation audit — three things the other side might hold against you — and open by naming one.
  • On your next call, mirror at least twice and stay quiet afterward. Notice how much extra they volunteer.
  • Replace one "Why did you…?" with a "How" or "What" calibrated question.
  • When you sense an unspoken objection, label it: "It seems like the timing feels risky."
  • If you reach a number, anchor with the Ackerman ladder instead of splitting the difference.

The deepest lesson is also the simplest: the best negotiators are not the loudest talkers, they are the most disciplined listeners. Information is leverage, and people hand it to whoever makes them feel heard.

---

Attribution: Principles drawn from Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It by Chris Voss with Tahl Raz (Harper Business, 2016). This entry is an original summary and commentary, not a reproduction of the text.
